html.fn_date.from:
date.from()

FunctionIn the guide

Builds a timestamp from calendar fields, read as a wall clock time in the chart's timezone unless zone names another. Use it for a fixed date, such as the start of a period you want to study.

Syntax

date.from(
    year: number,
    month: number,
    day: number,
    hour?: number = 0,
    minute?: number = 0,
    second?: number = 0,
    zone?: string = chart.timezone
) -> number

Arguments

yearnumberRequired

The calendar year, such as 2025. Every field must be a whole number, or the result is none.

monthnumberRequired

The month, 1 for January through 12 for December. A value outside that range rolls over, so 13 is January of the next year.

daynumberRequired

The day of the month, 1 to 31. A value outside the month rolls over, so day 0 is the last day of the month before.

hournumberDefault 0

The hour on a 24 hour clock, 0 to 23.

minutenumberDefault 0

The minute of the hour, 0 to 59.

secondnumberDefault 0

The second of the minute, 0 to 59.

zonestringDefault chart.timezone

The IANA timezone the fields are read in as a wall clock time, such as "Asia/Kolkata". Left out, the chart's timezone is used.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Every field must be a whole number, or the result is none. A field outside its normal range is not refused; it rolls over into the next unit. Month 13 is January of the next year, day 0 is the last day of the month before, and hour 25 is 01:00 the next day. Keep each field in its normal range unless that roll-over is what you want.

Examples

version 1
study("Since 1 January 2025", overlay = true)

start = date.from(2025, 1, 1, 9, 15)
plot(time >= start ? close : none, "Close since the start date", aqua)

See also

date.format(), input()

html.fn_date.isSameDay:
date.isSameDay()

FunctionIn the guide

True when two timestamps fall on the same calendar day in the chart's timezone. It compares the whole date, so two bars a month apart are never the same day. When either timestamp is absent, the answer is none.

Syntax

date.isSameDay(a: number, b: number, zone?: string = chart.timezone) -> bool

Arguments

anumberRequired

The first timestamp to compare, such as time.

bnumberRequired

The second timestamp to compare, such as time[1]. When either timestamp is absent, the answer is none.

dema()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The double exponential moving average subtracts an average's own lag once: 2 * ema - ema(ema). It hugs price more closely than ema() of the same length.

dema(src: series number, len: number) -> series number

Arguments

The series to average, such as close or another indicator's output.

lennumberRequired

The length of each of the two exponential averages.

html.fn_donchian:
donchian()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

Donchian channels: the highest high and lowest low of the last len bars, with the midpoint between them. A close beyond the previous bar's channel is a breakout, the basis of many trend-following systems. It returns [upper, basis, lower], upper first.

Syntax

donchian(len?: number = 20) -> array<number>

Arguments

lennumberDefault 20

The window, in bars, whose highest high and lowest low form the channel. It includes the current bar.

Returns

array<number>

First value: all elements at bar len - 1.

Remarks

The window includes the current bar, so the close can never be above this bar's upper line. Test a breakout against the previous bar's channel, upper[1], as the example does. The middle value is (upper + lower) / 2. All three start on bar len - 1.

Examples

version 1
study("Donchian breakout", overlay = true)

len = input(20, "Length", min = 2, max = 500)

dc    = donchian(len)
upper = dc[0]
lower = dc[2]

plot(upper, "Upper", lime, style = "step")
plot(dc[1], "Middle", fade(gray, 40), style = "step")
plot(lower, "Lower", red, style = "step")

if close > upper[1]
    signal("BREAKOUT", color = lime, at = "below", shape = "triangleUp")
if close < lower[1]
    signal("BREAKDOWN", color = red, at = "above", shape = "triangleDown")

dpo()

dpo(src: series number, len?: number = 21) -> series number

Arguments

The series to detrend, usually close.

lennumberDefault 21

The length of the simple average that is subtracted. The average is read as it stood floor(len / 2) + 1 bars ago.

Returns

series number

First value: bar len + floor(len / 2).

Remarks

The reading is src - sma(src, len)[floor(len / 2) + 1]: this bar's value less the simple average as it stood floor(len / 2) + 1 bars ago. It is reported on the current bar, not drawn back in time. The first value is on bar len + floor(len / 2), bar 31 for a length of 21.

html.fn_draw.box:
draw.box()

FunctionIn the guide

Creates a rectangle between two corners, (t1, p1) and (t2, p2), and returns it. A box is the shape for a price band over a stretch of time: a supply or demand zone, an opening range, the range of a mother bar. It can carry a caption inside it and a tooltip.

Syntax

draw.box(
    t1: number,
    p1: number,
    t2: number,
    p2: number,
    color?: color = none,
    fillColor?: color = none,
    opacity?: number = 0.12,
    width?: number = 1,
    text?: string = "",
    textColor?: color = white,
    tooltip?: string = ""
) -> box

Arguments

t1numberRequired

The time of the first corner, a timestamp in UTC milliseconds such as time or time[n].

p1numberRequired

The price of the first corner, on the scale of the pane the study draws in.

t2numberRequired

The time of the opposite corner, a timestamp like t1.

p2numberRequired

The price of the opposite corner.

colorcolorDefault none

The border colour. Left as none, no border is drawn, so give a box a border or a fill for it to be seen.

fillColorcolorDefault none

The colour inside the box. Left as none, the box has no fill.

opacitynumberDefault 0.12

How strongly the fill is drawn: the fill shows at opacity times the colour's own strength, and the default is faint enough to leave the candles readable.

widthnumberDefault 1

The thickness of the border.

textstringDefault ""

A caption drawn inside the box.

textColorcolorDefault white

The colour of the caption.

tooltipstringDefault ""

Detail shown while the pointer rests on the box, so the caption can stay short.

Returns

box

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

color is the border and fillColor the inside; both default to none, which draws nothing, so a box needs at least one of them to be seen. opacity dims the fill and defaults to 0.12, faint enough to leave the candles readable. The caption is drawn in textColor, white by default. A box has no extend argument, so a box that should reach the current bar has its right edge moved there with draw.setTo() on each bar, which is one cheap call against one object. A regime with no top or bottom, such as "the first fifteen minutes", belongs in background(), not in a box.

Examples

version 1
study("Inside bar zones", overlay = true, precision = 2)

keep = input(10, "Zones to keep", min = 1, max = 100)

var zones = []

// An inside bar trades within the previous bar's range.
insideBar = high < high[1] and low > low[1]

if insideBar
    zone = draw.box(time[1], high[1], time, low[1], color = orange, fillColor = orange, text = "inside", textColor = orange)
    push(zones, zone)
    if size(zones) > keep
        draw.delete(shift(zones))

See also

draw.setBounds(), draw.setText(), draw.setFillColor(), Lines and boxes

html.fn_draw.delete:
draw.delete()

FunctionIn the guide

Removes one object from the chart. Any kind of object is accepted. After the call the handle is stale: assign none to the name on the same lines, so no later setter reaches a deleted object.

Syntax

draw.delete(obj: line, label, box or polyline) -> nothing

Arguments

objline, label, box or polylineRequired

The line, label, box or polyline to remove. none, or an object already deleted, does nothing; assign none to the name on the same lines so no later setter reaches the deleted object.

Returns

nothing

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

A setter given a deleted object is error OS4005, which stops the script on that bar and names the bar the object was deleted on. Deleting an object that sits in an array leaves the element in the array; draw.delete(shift(list)) deletes the oldest object and removes it from the list in one line. When removing several elements in a loop, walk the list downwards, for i = size(list) - 1 to 0 step -1, so a removal never skips the element after it.

Examples

version 1
study("Cross marker", overlay = true, precision = 2)

sma50 = sma(close, 50)

var marker = none

if crossUp(close, sma50)
    if not isNone(marker)
        draw.delete(marker)
    marker = draw.label(time, low, "cross", color = lime, textColor = black)

// Remove the marker once price falls back, and forget the handle with it.
if not isNone(marker) and close < sma50
    draw.delete(marker)
    marker = none

See also

draw.deleteAll(), shift(), remove()
html.fn_draw.deleteAll:
draw.deleteAll()

FunctionIn the guide

Removes every object this script has created. It is a reset: use it when the whole picture is out of date, or on the newest bar in a study that draws only a small set of objects for the current state.

Syntax

draw.deleteAll() -> nothing

Returns

nothing

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Calling it on every bar and redrawing works but wastes effort: it rebuilds every object on every bar of history to show the state of the last one. Every handle the script still holds is stale afterwards, so set the names you keep to none or clear the arrays that hold them.

Examples

version 1
study("Last three pivot highs", overlay = true, precision = 2)

ph = pivotHigh(high, 5, 5)

var pivotTimes  = []
var pivotPrices = []
if not isNone(ph)
    push(pivotTimes, time[5])
    push(pivotPrices, ph)
    if size(pivotTimes) > 3
        shift(pivotTimes)
        shift(pivotPrices)

if bar.isLast
    // A small picture of the current state: clear it and draw it again.
    draw.deleteAll()
    for i = 0 to size(pivotTimes) - 1
        draw.label(element(pivotTimes, i), element(pivotPrices, i), text(element(pivotPrices, i), 2), color = red)

See also

draw.delete(), draw.count()
html.fn_draw.label:
draw.label()

FunctionIn the guide

Creates a plate of text anchored at a time and a price, and returns it. A label is an object you own: use it for a caption that belongs at a point, such as a pivot's price or the current reading beside the newest bar. For a marker on the bar where an event happened, signal() is simpler, because a signal has no handle to manage.

Syntax

draw.label(
    t: number,
    p: number,
    text: string,
    color?: color = none,
    textColor?: color = white,
    align?: string = "center",
    tooltip?: string = ""
) -> label

Arguments

tnumberRequired

The time the label is anchored at, a timestamp in UTC milliseconds such as time or time[n].

pnumberRequired

The price the label is placed at, on the scale of the pane the study draws in. There is no pixel offset, so pad the price with a multiple of atr() to clear the candle.

textstringRequired

The caption. Keep it short and put the detail in tooltip.

colorcolorDefault none

The colour of the plate behind the text. Left as none, no plate is drawn and the text sits straight on the chart.

textColorcolorDefault white

The colour of the text. Pick one that reads on the plate, or on the chart when there is no plate.

alignstringDefault "center"

Which part of the plate sits on the anchor's time: "center" centres it, "left" puts its left edge there so it extends to the right, and "right" puts its right edge there so it extends to the left.

tooltipstringDefault ""

Detail shown while the pointer rests on the label.

Returns

label

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

A label is placed at the price you give it; there is no pixel offset anywhere in the language, so pad with a multiple of atr() to clear the candle. color is the plate and defaults to none, which draws no plate at all: the text then sits straight on the chart in textColor, white by default, so give a label a plate colour or a text colour that reads on your chart. align decides which part of the plate sits on the anchor's time: "center" (the default) centres it, "left" puts the plate's left edge there so it extends to the right, and "right" puts its right edge there so it extends to the left. Keep the caption short and put detail in tooltip, which shows while the pointer rests on the label. text() of an absent value is the string "none", so guard captions built from values that may still be warming up. A label per bar is the commonest way to make a chart slow: a value on every bar is a plot().

Examples

version 1
study("Pivot labels", overlay = true, precision = 2)

rightBars = input(5,   "Pivot right bars", min = 1, max = 50)
padding   = input(0.5, "Padding, in ATR",  min = 0, max = 5)
keep      = input(30,  "Labels to keep",   min = 1, max = 500)

pivotUp   = pivotHigh(high, 5, rightBars)
pivotDown = pivotLow(low, 5, rightBars)

// Padding measured in the instrument's own volatility clears the bar on
// a stock at 250 and on an index future at 25,000 alike.
pad = atr(14) * padding

var tags = []

if not isNone(pivotUp)
    push(tags, draw.label(time[rightBars], pivotUp + pad, text(pivotUp, 2), color = red, textColor = white))

if not isNone(pivotDown)
    push(tags, draw.label(time[rightBars], pivotDown - pad, text(pivotDown, 2), color = lime, textColor = black))

// A pivot high and a pivot low can land on one bar, so trim until the list fits.
while size(tags) > keep
    draw.delete(shift(tags))

See also

draw.setAt(), draw.setText(), signal(), Labels and shapes
html.fn_draw.line:
draw.line()

FunctionIn the guide

Creates a straight line between two anchors, (t1, p1) and (t2, p2), and returns it. Use it for trendlines, a line joining two pivots, or a horizontal line that starts and stops rather than crossing the whole pane. extendLeft and extendRight continue it past its anchors to the edge of the pane.

Syntax

draw.line(
    t1: number,
    p1: number,
    t2: number,
    p2: number,
    color?: color = gray,
    width?: number = 1,
    style?: string = "solid",
    extendLeft?: bool = false,
    extendRight?: bool = false
) -> line

Arguments

t1numberRequired

The time of the first anchor, a timestamp in UTC milliseconds such as time or time[n].

p1numberRequired

The price of the first anchor, on the scale of the pane the study draws in.

t2numberRequired

The time of the second anchor, a timestamp like t1.

p2numberRequired

The price of the second anchor.

colorcolorDefault gray

The line colour.

widthnumberDefault 1

The line thickness.

stylestringDefault "solid"

The line pattern: "solid", "dashed" or "dotted".

One of "solid", "dashed", "dotted".

extendLeftboolDefault false

true continues the line past its first anchor to the left edge of the pane.

extendRightboolDefault false

true continues the line past its second anchor to the right edge of the pane, which is how a line reaches into the space past the newest bar.

Returns

line

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Anchor a pivot at time[rightBars], the bar it formed on, not at time, the bar it was reported on. An extended line needs no upkeep: its anchors fix the slope and the chart draws the rest. To reach into the empty space past the newest bar, extend the line rather than computing a future timestamp: time - time[1] is the bar length inside a session but the whole overnight gap on a session's first bar.

Examples

version 1
study("Pivot low trendline", overlay = true, precision = 2)

rightBars = input(5, "Pivot right bars", min = 1, max = 50)

pl = pivotLow(low, 5, rightBars)

var prevTime  = none
var prevPrice = none
var trend     = none

if not isNone(pl)
    // A pivot is reported rightBars bars late, so anchor it where it formed.
    pivotTime = time[rightBars]
    if not isNone(prevTime)
        if isNone(trend)
            trend = draw.line(prevTime, prevPrice, pivotTime, pl, color = lime, width = 2, extendRight = true)
        else
            draw.setBounds(trend, prevTime, prevPrice, pivotTime, pl)
    prevTime  = pivotTime
    prevPrice = pl

See also

draw.setBounds(), draw.setExtend(), draw.setStyle(), Lines and boxes
html.fn_draw.polyline:
draw.polyline()

FunctionIn the guide

Creates one path through many points and returns it. The points come as two arrays of the same length, one of times and one of prices, paired by index. With closed = true the path returns to its first point, and with a fillColor it becomes a filled shape: a wedge, a triangle, an outline around a range.

Syntax

draw.polyline(
    times: array<number>,
    prices: array<number>,
    color?: color = gray,
    width?: number = 1,
    closed?: bool = false,
    fillColor?: color = none,
    opacity?: number = 0.12
) -> polyline

Arguments

timesarray<number>Required

The times of the points, timestamps in UTC milliseconds, paired by index with prices. The path is copied when the call runs, so changing the array afterwards redraws nothing.

pricesarray<number>Required

The prices of the points, paired by index with times, so keep the two arrays the same length. A point whose time or price is none is a gap in the path.

colorcolorDefault gray

The colour of the path's stroke.

widthnumberDefault 1

The thickness of the stroke.

closedboolDefault false

true joins the last point back to the first, making a closed shape.

fillColorcolorDefault none

The colour inside the shape. Left as none, the shape has no fill.

opacitynumberDefault 0.12

How strongly the fill is drawn: the fill shows at opacity times the colour's own strength.

Returns

polyline

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

The path is copied when the call runs. Pushing to the arrays afterwards changes nothing on the chart; draw.setPoints() is how a path changes. Keep the two arrays the same length: trim both together. A point whose time or price is none is a gap: the path is drawn in separate pieces on either side of it, and on the /trading chart a path with a gap is drawn open and unfilled, whatever closed and fillColor say.

Examples

version 1
study("Last ten bars outline", overlay = true, precision = 2)

var outline = none

if bar.isLast
    times  = []
    prices = []
    // Along the highs, oldest first, then back along the lows.
    for i = 9 to 0 step -1
        push(times, time[i])
        push(prices, high[i])
    for i = 0 to 9
        push(times, time[i])
        push(prices, low[i])
    // One outline for the life of the chart: created once, then reshaped
    // as each new bar arrives.
    if isNone(outline)
        outline = draw.polyline(times, prices, color = purple, closed = true, fillColor = purple, opacity = 0.1)
    else
        draw.setPoints(outline, times, prices)

See also

draw.setPoints(), push(), Lines and boxes

draw.setExtend()

study("Support until broken", overlay = true, precision = 2)

draw.setFillColor()

The box's opacity, set when it was created, still dims the new colour.

version 1
study("First bar break", overlay = true, precision = 2)

// The session's first bar, or of the IST day where no session hours are stated.
newSession = orElse(session.isFirstBar, isNone(time[1]) or not date.isSameDay(time, time[1], "Asia/Kolkata"))

var zone   = none
var top    = none
var bottom = none

if newSession
    if not isNone(zone)
        draw.delete(zone)

    bottom = low

study("Session high line", overlay = true, precision = 2)

// The session's first bar, or of the IST day where no session hours are stated.

draw.setPoints()

Replaces the whole path of a polyline with new arrays of times and prices. A polyline keeps its own copy of the points it was given, so this call is the only way its shape changes.

draw.setPoints(
    polyline: polyline,
    times: array<number>,
    prices: array<number>

The polyline whose whole path is replaced.

timesarray<number>Required

The new times of the points, timestamps in UTC milliseconds, paired by index with prices.

The new prices of the points, paired by index with times.

version 1
study("Swing path", overlay = true, precision = 2)

rightBars = input(5,  "Pivot right bars", min = 1, max = 50)

pivotUp   = pivotHigh(high, 5, rightBars)
pivotDown = pivotLow(low, 5, rightBars)

var pathTimes  = []
var pathPrices = []

if not isNone(swing)
    push(pathTimes, time[rightBars])

draw.setStyle()

Changes a line to "solid", "dashed" or "dotted". Only a line has a style. A common use is to keep a level solid while it is in play and dash it once it has been reached.

Syntax

draw.setStyle(obj: line, style: string) -> nothing

Arguments

objlineRequired

The line to restyle. Only a line has a style.

The new line pattern: "solid", "dashed" or "dotted".

One of "solid", "dashed", "dotted".

Returns

nothing

study("Target line", overlay = true, precision = 2)

ema20 = ema(close, 20)
band  = atr(14)

var goal   = none
var hit    = false

html.fn_draw.setTextColor:
draw.setTextColor()

FunctionIn the guide

Changes the colour of the text in a label or a box. Pair it with draw.setColor() when a label's plate changes, so the text stays readable on it.

Syntax

draw.setTextColor(obj: label or box, color: color) -> nothing

Arguments

objlabel or boxRequired

The label or box whose text is recoloured.

colorcolorRequired

The new text colour.

Returns

nothing

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

rsi() and atr() are computed at the top level and only used inside the if. Called inside it, they would advance only on the newest bar and have no history. While the RSI is still none, the comparisons in ink are none too and take the false branch, so the text is black on the grey plate.

Examples

version 1
study("Current reading", overlay = true, precision = 2)

oscillator = rsi(close, 14)
pad        = atr(14)

fn show(value, decimals) => isNone(value) ? "warming up" : text(value, decimals)

var tag = none
if bar.isLast
    caption = "RSI " + show(oscillator, 1)
    plate   = isNone(oscillator) ? gray : (oscillator > 70 ? red : (oscillator < 30 ? lime : silver))
    // White reads on the red and green plates, black on grey and silver.
    ink     = oscillator > 70 or oscillator < 30 ? white : black
    if isNone(tag)
        tag = draw.label(time, high + pad, caption, color = plate, textColor = ink, tooltip = "14 bar RSI")
    else
        draw.setAt(tag, time, high + pad)
        draw.setText(tag, caption)
        draw.setColor(tag, plate)
        draw.setTextColor(tag, ink)

See also

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

An index outside 0 to size - 1, or with a fractional part, stops the study at that bar with OS4004. On a name that holds an array, [] reads an element and never an earlier bar. Where a line mixes the two meanings, element(arr, i) says which one you mean. The array returned by a multi-output function always has the same length, and each element is absent until its own warmup is over.

Examples

m = macd(close, 12, 26, 9)

plot(element(m, 0), "MACD", aqua)
plot(element(m, 1), "Signal", orange)
plot(m[2], "Histogram", gray, style = "histogram")

See also

size(), set(), indexOf()
html.fn_ema:
ema()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The exponential moving average gives the newest value a weight of 2 / (len + 1) and the running average the rest, so recent bars count more and old bars fade away without ever dropping out abruptly. It reacts to a new move sooner than sma() of the same length, which makes it the usual choice for crossover systems.

Syntax

ema(src: series number, len: number) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series to average, such as close or another indicator's output.

lennumberRequired

The length in bars. It sets the newest value's weight, 2 / (len + 1), and the bar the average is seeded on, len - 1.

Returns

series number

First value: bar len - 1.

Remarks

The average is seeded on bar len - 1 with the simple average of the first len values, and is absent before that. It does not start from the first close and drift into shape, so the line you see is correct from its first point. Each later bar computes value * weight + previous * (1 - weight). With len of 9 the newest close carries 20 percent of the weight. If the source is absent on a bar after the seed, that bar's result is absent and the running value is held, so the next present bar carries on where the last one left off.

Examples

version 1
study("EMA 9 and 21", overlay = true)

fastLen = input(9, "Fast", min = 1, max = 200)
slowLen = input(21, "Slow", min = 2, max = 400)

fast = ema(close, fastLen)
slow = ema(close, slowLen)

fastPlot = plot(fast, "EMA fast", aqua, width = 2)
slowPlot = plot(slow, "EMA slow", orange, width = 2)
fill(fastPlot, slowPlot, colorUp = fade(lime, 88), colorDown = fade(red, 88))

if crossUp(fast, slow)
    signal("BUY", color = lime, at = "below", shape = "arrowUp")
if crossDown(fast, slow)
    signal("SELL", color = red, at = "above", shape = "arrowDown")

The picture shows a 20 and 50 bar variant of this study on a daily SBIN chart, with the band shaded the same way and each crossing labelled Golden cross or Death cross in place of an arrow:

See also

sma(), rma(), dema(), tema(), crossUp()
html.fn_eom:
eom()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

Ease of movement: how far the bar's midpoint moved per unit of volume, averaged over len bars. A large positive reading means price rose easily on light volume; a reading near zero means it took heavy volume to move price at all.

Syntax

eom(len?: number = 14) -> series number

Arguments

lennumberDefault 14

The number of bars the per-bar ease of movement is averaged over.

Returns

series number

First value: bar len.

Remarks

Each bar's term is (hl2 - hl2[1]) * (high - low) / volume, and the result is its sma() over len, first available on bar len. No scaling constant is applied, so on a liquid NSE stock, where volume runs to lakhs of shares, the raw reading is very small. Multiply it at the plot to bring it into a readable range, as the example does with an input.

Examples

version 1
study("Ease of movement", precision = 2)

scale = input(100000, "Display scale", min = 1)
e     = eom(14) * scale

plot(e, "EOM", e >= 0 ? lime : red, width = 2)
level(0, "Zero", fade(gray, 60))

See also

forceIndex(), hl2
html.fn_exit:
exit()

FunctionStrategy onlyIn the guide

Sets the position's protective stop and profit target. Give the levels as prices (stop, limit) or as distances from the entry price in the instrument's own price units (loss, profit). A position carries at most one stop and one target, and calling exit again replaces them. A stop and a target sent together like this are called a bracket.

In version 0.5.0 the levels are not filled: the chart and the Backtest panel hand them on and never act on them, and the Strategies panel refuses to start a strategy that calls exit. So this example sends the levels with the entry and also tests them itself, which is what closes its trades today:

Syntax

exit(
    tag?: string = "",
    qty?: number = none,
    limit?: number = none,
    stop?: number = none,
    profit?: number = none,
    loss?: number = none,
    leg?: string
) -> nothing

Arguments

tagstringDefault ""

A label telling the destination which entry the levels protect. A tag that matches no order is not refused.

qtynumberDefault none

The quantity the stop and target are sent for, counted in the declaration's qtyType.

limitnumberDefault none

The profit target as a price. It cannot be given together with profit (OS3010).

stopnumberDefault none

The protective stop as a price, below a long and above a short. A level on the wrong side of an open position is refused with OS7010.

profitnumberDefault none

The profit target as a distance from the entry price, in the instrument's own price units. It cannot be given together with limit (OS3010).

lossnumberDefault none

The stop as a distance from the entry price, in the instrument's own price units. It cannot be given together with stop (OS3010).

legstringOptional

The leg the order is for, in a multi-leg strategy. Legs are planned, so writing it today is refused with OS3023.

Returns

nothing

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Four rules apply:

  • One side, one form. A price and a distance for the same side, such as stop with loss, is refused before the first bar with OS3010. A stop as a price and a target as a distance is fine.
  • An absent level is refused. exit is an order call, so a level whose value is absent is OS7002. The whole bar's orders go with it, including an entry placed on the line above, so test levels before you use them, as both examples do.
  • The right side of the position. A stop belongs below a long and above a short, a target the other way round. A level on the wrong side of an open position's average price is refused with OS7010. It is checked only against a position that is open, so an entry and its bracket on the same bar are the ordinary shape.
  • The tag is a label. It tells the destination which entry the levels protect. A tag that matches no order is not refused.

There is no trailing stop argument: the language's trailing stop is leg.trail(), which is planned. Exits and brackets covers exits in full, including a trailing stop written in the script.

Examples

version 1
strategy("Stop and target at entry", overlay = true, precision = 2, qty = 1)

atrValue = atr(14)
goLong   = crossUp(ema(close, 9), ema(close, 21))

stopPrice   = roundToTick(close - 2 * atrValue)
targetPrice = roundToTick(close + 4 * atrValue)
ready       = not isNone(stopPrice) and not isNone(targetPrice)

// The levels sent with the entry, kept so the script can test them as well.
var stopLevel   = none
var targetLevel = none

if goLong and pos.isFlat and ready
    buy(tag = "entry")
    exit(tag = "entry", stop = stopPrice, limit = targetPrice)
    stopLevel   = stopPrice
    targetLevel = targetPrice
else if pos.isLong and (low <= stopLevel or high >= targetLevel)
    close()

plot(pos.isFlat ? none : stopLevel, "Stop", red, style = "step")
plot(pos.isFlat ? none : targetLevel, "Target", lime, style = "step")

The distance form suits a market entry, whose fill price your script does not know yet. The levels travel as distances and are measured from the fill:

atrValue = atr(14)

if crossUp(ema(close, 9), ema(close, 21)) and pos.isFlat and not isNone(atrValue)
    buy(tag = "entry")
    exit(tag = "entry", loss = 2 * atrValue, profit = 4 * atrValue)

See also

order.bracket(), close(), leg.stop(), leg.target()

html.fn_fade:
fade()

FunctionIn the guide

The same colour made percent transparent, where 0 leaves it unchanged and 100 makes it invisible. It is the call most scripts reach for when shading a fill or a background.

Syntax

fade(color: color, percent: number) -> color

Arguments

colorcolorRequired

The colour to make transparent. The alpha it already has is scaled, so fading twice compounds.

percentnumberRequired

How transparent to make it, from 0 (unchanged) to 100 (invisible).

Returns

color

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

fade scales the alpha the colour already has: the result's alpha is alpha(color) * (100 - percent) / 100. On an opaque colour that is simply (100 - percent) / 100, but fading twice compounds, so fade(fade(aqua, 50), 50) has an alpha of 0.25, not 0.5. Apply fade once, to an opaque colour, or use withAlpha() to set an exact alpha.

A computed percent outside 0 to 100 is not refused. The resulting alpha is kept within 0 to 1, so a percent above 100 gives an invisible colour and a negative one makes the colour more opaque. Hold a computed percent in range with clamp().

As a guide, a fill between two plots wants roughly fade(c, 85) to fade(c, 95), and a whole-bar background() more than that.

Examples

b = bollinger(close, 20, 2)
upper = plot(b[1], "Upper", aqua)
lower = plot(b[2], "Lower", aqua)
fill(upper, lower, fade(aqua, 88))

See also

withAlpha(), alpha(), fill(), background()

The series to test, such as an average or an oscillator.

lennumberRequired

How many consecutive one bar changes must all be below zero. A whole number of 1 or more; an unchanged bar breaks the run.

Returns

series bool

Remarks

html.fn_fill:
fill()

FunctionTop level onlyIn the guide

Shades the region between two plots. A band turns "which line is higher, and by how much" into a colour a reader takes in at a glance, which is why it suits a volatility band, a moving average cross, or an oscillator shaded to its midline. Its first two arguments are the handles that plot() or plotCandles() returned, not values.

Syntax

fill(
    plotA: plot,
    plotB: plot,
    color?: color = none,
    colorUp?: color = none,
    colorDown?: color = none,
    opacity?: number = 1,
    overlay?: bool = none
) -> fill

Arguments

plotAplotRequired

The first plot of the band: the handle a plot() or plotCandles() call returned, not a value. colorUp paints where this plot is above plotB.

plotBplotRequired

The second plot of the band, also a handle returned by plot() or plotCandles(). A value in its place is error OS3020.

colorcolorDefault none

One colour for the whole band. It cannot be given together with colorUp or colorDown (OS3010). With no colour given at all, the band takes plotA's colour faded to twelve percent.

colorUpcolorDefault none

The band's colour where plotA is above plotB.

colorDowncolorDefault none

The band's colour where plotA is below plotB.

opacitynumberDefault 1

A dimmer from 0 to 1 that multiplies whatever transparency the colours already have. Dimming with both opacity and fade() compounds, so pick one.

Fixed before the first bar.

overlayboolDefault none

true draws the band on the price pane. The band and the two plots it names must end up in the same pane, which the compiler does not check.

Fixed before the first bar.

Returns

fill

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

A band stops wherever either of its plots is none and resumes where both return, so it inherits their warmup with no code from you. opacity is a dimmer from 0 to 1 that multiplies whatever transparency the colours already have. It defaults to 1 and is fixed before the first bar; dimming with both opacity and fade() compounds, so pick one. A band and the two plots it names must end up in the same pane, and the compiler does not check it: give both plots the same overlay and offset, and the band the same overlay. On the /trading chart in this release a band takes one colour: a colour computed per bar, such as color = squeezed ? orange : none, is not applied bar by bar, and the band is drawn in plotA's colour faded instead. To switch a band off on some bars there, make one of its plots none on those bars.

Examples

version 1
study("EMA cross, shaded", overlay = true, precision = 2)

fast = ema(close, 9)
slow = ema(close, 21)

pFast = plot(fast, "Fast", aqua, width = 2)
pSlow = plot(slow, "Slow", orange, width = 2)

// pFast comes first, so colorUp paints where the FAST average is higher.
fill(pFast, pSlow, colorUp = fade(lime, 85), colorDown = fade(red, 85))
Colour argumentsThe band is
None of the threeplotA's colour, faded to twelve percent
colorThat colour on both sides
colorUp and colorDowncolorUp where plotA is above plotB, colorDown where it is below

Giving color together with colorUp or colorDown is error OS3010. Passing a value where a handle belongs is error OS3020:

pClose = plot(close, "Close")
fill(pClose, open)

To shade to a fixed value, which a level() cannot do, plot the value as a column and make it invisible. fade() takes a transparency in percent, so fade(c, 100) is fully transparent.

version 1
study("RSI shaded to 50", precision = 2, range = [0, 100])

pRsi = plot(rsi(close, 14), "RSI", purple, width = 2)
pMid = plot(50, "Midline", fade(gray, 100))
fill(pRsi, pMid, colorUp = fade(lime, 86), colorDown = fade(red, 86))

See also

plot(), level(), fade(), Fills

html.fn_highest:
highest()

highest(src: series number, len: number) -> series number

srcseries numberRequired

The series to search, usually high or close.

lennumberRequired

How many bars the window covers, this bar included. A whole number of 1 or more.

html.fn_highestBars:
highestBars()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

How many bars ago the highest value in the window was set: 0 when this bar set it, up to len - 1 when the oldest bar in the window did. Use it to ask how fresh a high is, or to find the bar a high was made on.

Syntax

highestBars(src: series number, len: number) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series to search, usually high.

lennumberRequired

How many bars the window covers, this bar included. A whole number of 1 or more.

Returns

series number

First value: bar len - 1.

Remarks

A tie goes to the most recent bar: when the same high is touched twice inside the window, the count is to the later touch. The result is a whole number of bars, so it works as an offset: close[highestBars(high, 50)] is the close on the bar that set the high, and time[highestBars(high, 50)] is that bar's time, which is where a drawing anchored to the high belongs.

html.fn_history:
history()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

src as it stood n bars ago: the call form of src[n]. It takes an expression directly, so history(close - open, 1) is the previous bar's body without naming it first.

Syntax

history(src: T, n: number) -> T

Arguments

srcTRequired

The value to read from an earlier bar: a series, an expression such as close - open, or an array.

nnumberRequired

How many bars back to read. A whole number of 1 or more; 0 stops the script with OS4003, where close[0] would simply read this bar.

Returns

T

First value: bar n.

Remarks

The first value is on bar n. Unlike the offset inside [], n is a length: a whole number of 1 or more, so history(close, 0) stops the script with OS4003 where close[0] simply reads this bar. Bars and history covers when to prefer a named value.

Numbers only in this release

In release 0.5.0 history returns a value only when src is a number. On a bool, a string or an array it compiles and gives none on every bar. For a bool or a string, name the value at the top level and use the operator instead: flag[1] works where history(flag, 1) does not.

html.fn_hma:
hma()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The Hull moving average combines weighted averages so that most of the lag cancels out: it follows price closely while staying smooth. Traders often colour it by its slope and treat a change of slope as a change of trend.

Syntax

hma(src: series number, len: number) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series to average, such as close or another indicator's output.

lennumberRequired

The length in bars. The recipe takes weighted averages over len, over half of it and over its rounded square root.

Returns

series number

First value: bar len + round(sqrt(len)) - 2.

Remarks

The recipe is wma(2 * wma(src, half) - wma(src, len), round(sqrt(len))), where half is floor(len / 2) held at a minimum of 1. The first value arrives on bar len + round(sqrt(len)) - 2, bar 60 for a length of 55. Because it removes lag by extrapolating, it can overshoot price at sharp turns.

Examples

version 1
study("Hull average", overlay = true)

len = input(55, "Length", min = 2, max = 500)
h = hma(close, len)

plot(h, "HMA", h > h[1] ? lime : red, width = 2)

See also

wma(), ema(), ma()
html.fn_hv:
hv()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

Historical volatility: the standard deviation of the bar-to-bar log returns, annualised. It is the realised counterpart of an option's implied volatility, so comparing the two on NIFTY or BANKNIFTY tells you whether options are pricing more or less movement than the index has actually shown. On Indian index options the implied side of that comparison comes from Black-76 pricing off the synthetic future; hv() gives you the realised side.

Syntax

hv(
    src: series number,
    len?: number = 20,
    periodsPerYear?: number = 252
) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series whose log returns are measured, usually close.

lennumberDefault 20

The number of log returns in the window.

periodsPerYearnumberDefault 252

How many of the chart's bars make a year, used to annualise the deviation: 252 for daily bars, or the bars in a session times the sessions in a year, such as 75 * 252 on a 5 minute chart.

Returns

series number

First value: bar len.

Remarks

The reading is stdev(log(src / src[1]), len) * sqrt(periodsPerYear), with the population deviation. It is a proportion, not a percentage: 0.18 means 18 percent a year, so the example multiplies by 100 at the plot. periodsPerYear is the number of the chart's bars in a year: 252 for daily bars, and for intraday NSE bars the bars in the 09:15 to 15:30 session times the sessions, for example 75 * 252 (18900) on a 5-minute chart. A log return needs the previous bar, so the first value is on bar len.

Examples

version 1
study("Historical volatility", precision = 2)

len     = input(20, "Length", min = 2, max = 500)
periods = input(252, "Bars per year", min = 1)

plot(hv(close, len, periods) * 100, "HV %", purple, width = 2)

See also

stdev(), natr(), log()
html.fn_ichimoku:
ichimoku()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The Ichimoku cloud: five lines that together describe trend, support and momentum. The conversion and base lines are the midpoints of the highest high and lowest low over 9 and 26 bars. Span A is the average of those two, span B is the 52 bar midpoint, and the space between the spans forms the cloud. The lagging line is the close. It returns [conversion, base, spanA, spanB, lagging].

Syntax

ichimoku(
    convLen?: number = 9,
    baseLen?: number = 26,
    spanLen?: number = 52
) -> array<number>

Arguments

convLennumberDefault 9

The window, in bars, whose highest high and lowest low give the conversion line.

baseLennumberDefault 26

The window, in bars, whose highest high and lowest low give the base line. It is also the usual displacement of the spans and the lagging line, so change the plot offsets to match.

spanLennumberDefault 52

The window, in bars, whose highest high and lowest low give span B.

Returns

array<number>

First value: element by element at bar convLen - 1, baseLen - 1, baseLen - 1, spanLen - 1, baseLen - 1.

Remarks

Each value has its own first bar: conversion on bar convLen - 1, base, span A and lagging on bar baseLen - 1, and span B on bar spanLen - 1 (bars 8, 25 and 51 with the defaults). Span A is the average of the conversion and base values, not a midpoint over a window of its own. Returning the spans unshifted means you can compare them with anything else in the script directly.

Examples

version 1
study("Ichimoku cloud", overlay = true)

ich = ichimoku(9, 26, 52)

plot(ich[0], "Conversion", aqua)
plot(ich[1], "Base", maroon)
spanA = plot(ich[2], "Span A", lime, offset = 26)
spanB = plot(ich[3], "Span B", red, offset = 26)
fill(spanA, spanB, colorUp = fade(lime, 85), colorDown = fade(red, 85))
plot(ich[4], "Lagging", gray, offset = -26)

The spans come back on the bar they are computed on, not shifted. The plot's offset draws them 26 bars forward and the lagging line 26 bars back, which is how the cloud is traditionally shown. If you change baseLen, change the offsets to match. To compare today's close with the part of the cloud drawn above today's bar, read the spans 26 bars back:

version 1
study("Close above the cloud", overlay = true)

ich   = ichimoku()
spanA = ich[2]
spanB = ich[3]

cloudTop = max(spanA[26], spanB[26])

background(close > cloudTop ? fade(lime, 92) : none)

See also

donchian(), plot(), Fills
html.fn_indexOf:
indexOf()

FunctionIn the guide

The index of the first element equal to v, or -1 when no element is. With two arrays kept side by side, it turns one into a lookup table for the other.

Syntax

indexOf(arr: array<E>, v: E) -> number

Arguments

arrarray<E>Required

The array to search.

vERequired

The value to look for, compared with ==. Search for none to find an absent element.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Not found is -1, a definite answer, so compare the result with -1 or >= 0. The search uses ==, so an absent element is found by searching for none, and two drawings match only when they are the same drawing. The search walks the array from the front, one element at a time.

Examples

names  = ["sma", "ema", "wma"]
lens   = [50, 21, 30]
choice = input("ema", "Average", options = ["sma", "ema", "wma"])

// Each average type has its own length, found by position.
slot = indexOf(names, choice)
len  = slot >= 0 ? element(lens, slot) : 20

plot(ma(close, len, choice), "Average")

See also

element(), str.indexOf(), arrayEqual()
html.fn_input:
input()

FunctionTop level onlyIn the guide

Declares one setting and returns its value. The first argument is the default, and its type decides the kind of row; the second is the row's label. The value is known before the first bar and is the same on every bar, so you can use it anywhere a plain value of its type fits.

Syntax

input(
    value: any,
    title?: string,
    min?: number,
    max?: number,
    step?: number,
    options?: array<string>,
    kind?: string,
    group?: string = "",
    tooltip?: string = "",
    inline?: string,
    confirm?: bool
) -> any

Arguments

valueanyRequired

The starting value, whose type decides the kind of row: a number gives a number field, true or false a tick box, text a text field, a colour a swatch, and a price series such as close a menu of price sources. It must be known before any data arrives.

titlestringOptional

The row's label in the settings dialog, written as text at the call. When the input is assigned to a name it may be left out, and the name becomes the label.

Fixed before the first bar.

minnumberOptional

For a number, the lowest value allowed. The arrows stop there, and a saved value below it stops the study from loading with OS6019.

Fixed before the first bar.

maxnumberOptional

For a number, the highest value allowed. The arrows stop there, and a saved value above it stops the study from loading with OS6019.

Fixed before the first bar.

stepnumberOptional

For a number, how far one click of an arrow moves the value. It shapes the arrows only: a value typed into the field is kept as typed.

Fixed before the first bar.

optionsarray<string>Optional

A list of strings that turns a text row into a menu of exactly those values. The default must be one of them, or the script is refused with OS3018.

Fixed before the first bar.

kindstringOptional

Picks a row the type alone cannot: "interval" builds a timeframe menu, and "time" a date and time field whose value is a timestamp. "symbol", "price" and "session" are planned, and writing one is error OS2001.

One of "interval", "time", "symbol", "price", "session". Fixed before the first bar.

groupstringDefault ""

A heading the row sits under. The settings dialog, and the input forms of the Backtest and Strategies panels, show each group as a heading over its rows.

Fixed before the first bar.

tooltipstringDefault ""

Help text shown as a line under the row: the unit, or what moving the value does.

Fixed before the first bar.

inlinestringOptional

Planned: rows given the same value would sit on one line. It is accepted and has no effect yet.

Fixed before the first bar.

confirmboolOptional

Planned: the value would be asked for when the study is added to a chart. It is accepted and has no effect yet.

Fixed before the first bar.

Returns

any

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

The settings dialog is built once, before the first bar, from the input() calls the compiler can see. Every rule about input() follows from that:

  • It is written at the top level of the file, outside any block: as an assignment, inside a larger expression, as a declaration option such as study("B", precision = input(2, "Decimals")), or inside the expression of a req.timeframe() read. Inside an if, a loop or a function it is OS3007.
  • The default is fixed before any data arrives: a literal, arithmetic over literals, a colour built from literals such as fade(aqua, 50), or, for a source, one of the price series. A default computed from bar data is OS3003.
  • The title is written as a string literal on the line. When the input is assigned to a name, the title can be left out and defaults to that name.
  • An input has no warmup: its value exists on bar 0.

Examples

len  = input(20, "Length", min = 2, max = 500)
mult = input(2.0, "Band width, in standard deviations", min = 0.5, max = 5, step = 0.1)

basis = sma(close, len)
dev   = mult * stdev(close, len)

plot(basis, "Basis", orange)
plot(basis + dev, "Upper", aqua)
plot(basis - dev, "Lower", aqua)

See also

ma(), req.timeframe(), table(), Declarations
html.fn_insert:
insert()

FunctionIn the guide

Adds v before index i, moving that element and everything after it up by one. Use it to keep an array in order as values arrive.

Syntax

insert(arr: array<E>, i: number, v: E) -> nothing

Arguments

arrarray<E>Required

The array to insert into.

inumberRequired

The index to insert before, from 0 to size(arr). Inserting at size(arr) adds to the end; anything larger is OS4004.

vERequired

The value to insert, of the array's element type.

Returns

nothing

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

i may be from 0 to size(arr); inserting at size(arr) adds to the end, like push(). Anything larger is OS4004.

Examples

// The ten widest bars seen so far, widest first.
var widest: array<number> = []
barRange = high - low

i = 0
while i < size(widest) and element(widest, i) >= barRange
    i += 1

if i < 10
    insert(widest, i, barRange)
    if size(widest) > 10
        pop(widest)

// Drawn once ten bars have been seen, so the line is always the tenth widest.
plot(size(widest) == 10 ? element(widest, 9) : none, "Tenth widest bar so far")

See also

remove(), push(), unshift()
html.fn_isNone:
isNone()

FunctionIn the guide

True when the value is absent, and false for any present value of any type. It is the same test as x == none; use whichever reads better.

Syntax

isNone(x: any) -> bool

Arguments

xanyRequired

The value to test, of any type.

Returns

bool

First value: bar 0, whatever its arguments.

Remarks

isNone always answers true or false, from bar 0, whatever its argument. That is why it is safe as a guard on the left of and: in not isNone(x) and x > 5, the comparison runs only when x is present.

Order matters for which side runs, not for the answer. not isNone(x) and x > 5 and x > 5 and not isNone(x) give the same result; isNone(x) and x > 5 is never true however you write it.

Examples

version 1
study("Warmup shading", overlay = true)

slow = sma(close, 200)
background(isNone(slow) ? fade(gray, 90) : none)
plot(slow, "SMA 200", orange)

See also

orElse(), bar.isFirst
html.fn_keltner:
keltner()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

Keltner channels: a moving average of the close with bands a multiple of the average true range above and below it. Where Bollinger Bands widen with the spread of closes, Keltner channels widen with how far the bars actually travel, which makes them steadier. It returns [basis, upper, lower].

Syntax

keltner(
    len?: number = 20,
    mult?: number = 2,
    atrLen?: number = 10,
    maType?: string = "ema"
) -> array<number>

Arguments

lennumberDefault 20

The length of the average of the close that forms the basis.

multnumberDefault 2

How many average true ranges the upper and lower bands sit from the basis.

atrLennumberDefault 10

The length of the average true range that sets the width of the bands.

maTypestringDefault "ema"

Which average forms the basis: "sma", "ema", "wma", "rma", "hma" or "vwma". Another name is not caught when the script compiles and leaves all three values absent on every bar.

Returns

array<number>

First value: all elements at bar max(len, atrLen) - 1.

Remarks

The basis is the average of the close over len, of the type maType names: "sma", "ema", "wma", "rma", "hma" or "vwma", as in ma(). The width is atr(atrLen), and the bands are basis + mult * atr and basis - mult * atr. All three values start on bar max(len, atrLen) - 1. The compiler does not check maType; a name that is not one of the six leaves all three values absent on every bar.

Examples

version 1
study("Keltner channel and squeeze", overlay = true)

len  = input(20, "Length", min = 2, max = 500)
mult = input(1.5, "ATR multiple", min = 0.5, max = 5, step = 0.25)

kc = keltner(len, mult, 10, "ema")
bb = bollinger(close, len, 2)

plot(kc[0], "Basis", orange)
upper = plot(kc[1], "Upper", teal)
lower = plot(kc[2], "Lower", teal)
fill(upper, lower, fade(teal, 92))

squeezed = bb[1] < kc[1] and bb[2] > kc[2]
background(squeezed ? fade(yellow, 90) : none)

The background marks a squeeze: the Bollinger Bands sitting inside the Keltner channel. During warmup either side of the comparison is absent, the condition takes the false branch, and nothing is painted.

See also

bollinger(), atr(), ma(), donchian()
html.fn_level:
level()

FunctionTop level onlyIn the guide

Draws one horizontal line straight across the study's pane at one price: 70 and 30 on an oscillator, zero under a histogram, yesterday's high on a price chart. A level takes no column, has no history and shows no value in the legend, which is what makes it the right tool for a threshold and the wrong one for a measurement.

Syntax

level(
    price: series number,
    title?: string = "",
    color?: color = #808080ff,
    style?: string = "dashed",
    width?: number = 1
) -> level

Arguments

priceseries numberRequired

The price the horizontal line is drawn at. It is read on every bar and the line drawn is the one from the last bar executed, so an absent price on the newest bar draws no line.

titlestringDefault ""

The line's name. Give every level one, since it is the line's only label: a level shows no value in the legend.

Fixed before the first bar.

colorcolorDefault #808080ff

The line's colour, one colour fixed for the whole chart.

Fixed before the first bar.

stylestringDefault "dashed"

The line pattern: "solid", "dashed" or "dotted".

One of "solid", "dashed", "dotted". Fixed before the first bar.

widthnumberDefault 1

The line thickness.

Fixed before the first bar.

Returns

level

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

An absent price on the last bar draws no line, which is the way to switch a level off, for example pos.isFlat ? none : pos.avgPrice in a strategy. A level cannot be one end of a fill() (error OS3020); plot the value instead, fully transparent if the line itself should not show. When you want to see where a value used to be, it is not a level: draw it with plot(x, "Title", style = "step"). Give every level a title, since it is the line's only label.

Examples

version 1
study("RSI with zones", precision = 2, range = [0, 100])

len = input(14, "Length", min = 2, max = 200)

level(70, "Overbought", fade(red, 40))
level(50, "Middle", fade(gray, 70), style = "dotted")
level(30, "Oversold", fade(lime, 40))

plot(rsi(close, len), "RSI", purple, width = 2)

The price may be computed from the data. It is read on every bar, and the line drawn is the one from the last bar executed. So a price that exists on only one bar usually draws nothing: hold it in a var instead.

version 1
study("Session open", overlay = true, precision = 2)

// The session's first bar, or the first bar of the IST day where the host
// states no session hours.
newSession = orElse(session.isFirstBar, isNone(time[1]) or not date.isSameDay(time, time[1], "Asia/Kolkata"))

var sessionOpen = none
if newSession
    sessionOpen = open

// Held, so the newest bar has a price to draw.
level(sessionOpen, "Session open", fade(aqua, 25), style = "solid", width = 2)

See also

plot(), fill(), Levels, Declarations

lime

Constantrgb(0, 255, 0)In the guide

Pure, bright green. The conventional colour for a rising bar, a bullish signal and a breakout.

Type

color

barColor(close > high[1] ? lime : none)

html.fn_linreg:
linreg()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The linear regression value: fit a least squares straight line through the last len values and return the line's value on this bar. It tracks a steady trend closely, and the line's slope tells you how fast the trend is moving.

Syntax

linreg(src: series number, len: number, offset?: number = 0) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series the straight line is fitted through.

lennumberRequired

The number of bars the least squares line is fitted over.

offsetnumberDefault 0

How many bars back along the fitted line to read it. 0 reads it on the current bar, so linreg(src, len) - linreg(src, len, 1) is the slope per bar.

Returns

series number

First value: bar len - 1.

Remarks

The fit places the oldest bar of the window at 0 and this bar at len - 1. offset reads the same fitted line offset bars back without fitting it again, so linreg(src, len) - linreg(src, len, 1) is the slope per bar, as the example uses it. A length of 1 has no line to fit and returns none on every bar.

Examples

version 1
study("Regression line and slope", overlay = true)

len = input(50, "Length", min = 2, max = 500)

fitted = linreg(close, len)
slope  = fitted - linreg(close, len, 1)

plot(fitted, "Regression", slope > 0 ? lime : red, width = 2)

See also

sma(), correlation()
html.fn_log:
log()

FunctionIn the guide

The natural logarithm of x, and none when x is zero or below. Use it for log returns, which add up across bars, or for a log scale of price.

Syntax

log(x: number) -> number

Arguments

xnumberRequired

The number whose natural logarithm is taken. Zero or below gives none.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Log returns add: the sum of the last 20 one bar log returns equals log(close / close[20]), which plain percentage returns do not. log(0) and log(-1) give none.

Examples

version 1
study("Log return", precision = 4)

ret = log(close) - log(close[1])
plot(ret * 100, "Log return, %", aqua, style = "histogram")
plot(sum(ret, 20) * 100, "20 bar log return, %", orange)

exp(), log10(), math.log2()
html.fn_log10:
log10()

FunctionIn the guide

The base ten logarithm of x, with the same rule as log(): none at zero or below. Use it to read a quantity in orders of magnitude.

log10(x: number) -> number

Arguments

xnumberRequired

The number whose base ten logarithm is taken. Zero or below gives none.

Returns

number

Remarks

log10(1000) is 3. On an instrument without volume, such as an index, volume is absent and so is the line.

study("Turnover in powers of ten", precision = 2)

// Rupee turnover of the bar: 5 is one lakh, 7 is one crore.

level(7, "One crore", gray)

lowest()

The smallest value of src over the last len bars, this bar included. Use it for the bottom of a range, a support level, or a stop below recent lows.

lennumberRequired

html.fn_ma:
ma()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

One call for six averages, chosen by name: "sma", "ema", "wma", "rma", "hma" or "vwma". Feed type from an input() with those options and the user can switch the average from the study's settings dialog without editing the script.

Syntax

ma(src: series number, len: number, type?: string = "sma") -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series to average, such as close or another indicator's output.

lennumberRequired

The length in bars, passed to the average type names.

typestringDefault "sma"

Which average to compute: "sma", "ema", "wma", "rma", "hma" or "vwma". Feed it from a select input so the reader can switch the average in the settings dialog.

One of "sma", "ema", "wma", "rma", "hma", "vwma".

Returns

series number

First value: the named type's.

Remarks

The result and its first value are exactly those of the named average. A literal type that is not one of the six is error OS3008 when you compile. A type that only arrives while the script runs and names none of the six gives none on every bar rather than silently drawing a different average. Each type keeps its own state, so switching type starts the new average from its own seed.

Examples

version 1
study("Switchable average", overlay = true)

kind = input("ema", "Average", options = ["sma", "ema", "wma", "rma", "hma", "vwma"])
len  = input(20, "Length", min = 1, max = 500)

plot(ma(close, len, kind), "Average", aqua, width = 2)

See also

sma(), ema(), keltner(), Inputs
html.fn_macd:
macd()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

Moving average convergence divergence: the gap between a fast and a slow ema() of the source. It returns [macd, signal, histogram]: the gap itself, an ema() of the gap, and the difference between the two. The line crossing its signal and the histogram crossing zero are the classic momentum turns.

Syntax

macd(
    src: series number,
    fast?: number = 12,
    slow?: number = 26,
    signal?: number = 9
) -> array<number>

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series both averages are taken of, usually close.

fastnumberDefault 12

The length of the fast exponential average.

slownumberDefault 26

The length of the slow exponential average, which is subtracted from the fast one.

signalnumberDefault 9

The length of the exponential average of the MACD line that forms the signal line.

Returns

array<number>

First value: element 0 at bar max(fast, slow) - 1, elements 1 and 2 at bar max(fast, slow) + signal - 2.

Remarks

The line is ema(src, fast) - ema(src, slow). The signal average is fed the line from its first value, so it seeds on the first signal values the line produced, and the histogram is line - signal as reported. With the defaults the line starts on bar 25 and the signal and histogram on bar 33. The line is in price units, so a stock near 3,000 shows a much larger MACD than one near 300; use ppo() to compare them. Give the signal line a name other than signal: that is a library function, and assigning to it is error OS2002.

Examples

version 1
study("MACD", precision = 2)

fastLen   = input(12, "Fast", min = 1, max = 200)
slowLen   = input(26, "Slow", min = 2, max = 400)
signalLen = input(9, "Signal", min = 1, max = 100)

m    = macd(close, fastLen, slowLen, signalLen)
line = m[0]
sig  = m[1]
hist = m[2]

plot(hist, "Histogram", hist >= 0 ? fade(lime, 40) : fade(red, 40), style = "histogram")
plot(line, "MACD", aqua, width = 2)
plot(sig, "Signal", orange)
level(0, "Zero", fade(gray, 60))

if crossUp(line, sig)
    signal("MACD UP", color = lime, at = "below", shape = "triangleUp")

See also

ppo(), ema(), crossUp()

html.fn_math.acos:
math.acos()

FunctionIn the guide

The angle, in radians, whose cosine is x, from 0 to math.pi. Gives none when x is outside -1 to 1.

Syntax

math.acos(x: number) -> number

Arguments

xnumberRequired

The cosine to turn back into an angle, from -1 to 1. Outside that range gives none.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

math.acos(-1) is math.pi and math.acos(1) is 0. As with math.asin(), keep the clamp() on a ratio that should be in range by construction. The example needs an instrument with volume.

Examples

version 1
study("Angle between range and volume", precision = 0, range = [0, 180])

// A correlation is the cosine of the angle between the two windows once each
// has had its mean removed. acos turns it back into that angle:
// 0 degrees moves together, 90 unrelated, 180 opposite.
rho = correlation(high - low, volume, 50)

// clamp guards against a rounding error that lands a hair outside -1 to 1.
plot(math.toDegrees(math.acos(clamp(rho, -1, 1))), "Angle, degrees", aqua)
level(90, "Unrelated", gray)

html.fn_math.asin:
math.asin()

FunctionIn the guide

The angle, in radians, whose sine is x, from -math.pi / 2 to math.pi / 2. Gives none when x is outside -1 to 1. Use it to turn a ratio between -1 and 1 back into an angle.

Syntax

math.asin(x: number) -> number

Arguments

xnumberRequired

The sine to turn back into an angle, from -1 to 1. Outside that range gives none.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Keep the clamp() even when the ratio should be in range by construction. A binary rounding error can put it a hair outside -1 to 1, and then the result is none for that bar.

Examples

version 1
study("Close position as an angle", precision = 0, range = [-90, 90])

// Where the close sits in the bar's range: -1 at the low, 1 at the high.
barRange = high - low
position = barRange > 0 ? (2 * close - high - low) / barRange : none

plot(math.toDegrees(math.asin(clamp(position, -1, 1))), "Angle", aqua)

See also

math.sin(), math.acos(), clamp()
html.fn_math.atan:
math.atan()

FunctionIn the guide

The angle, in radians, whose tangent is x, from -math.pi / 2 to math.pi / 2. Every number has one, so it never gives none for a present x. Use it to squash a value that can grow without limit into a fixed range.

Syntax

math.atan(x: number) -> number

Arguments

xnumberRequired

The tangent to turn back into an angle. Any present number is accepted.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

math.atan(1) is math.pi / 4, 45 degrees. For an angle from a rise and a run, where the run can be zero or negative, use math.atan2().

Examples

version 1
study("Bounded z-score", precision = 2, range = [-1, 1])

z = (close - sma(close, 50)) / stdev(close, 50)

// atan maps any number into -pi / 2 to pi / 2, so this line stays inside
// -1 to 1 however far the close runs from its average.
plot(2 / math.pi * math.atan(z), "Bounded z", aqua)
level(0, "Zero", gray)

math.atan2(), math.tan(), math.toDegrees()
html.fn_math.atan2:
math.atan2()

FunctionIn the guide

The angle, in radians, of the point (x, y) seen from the origin, from -math.pi to math.pi. Note the order: y comes first. Unlike math.atan(y / x), it tells the four quarters of the circle apart and works when x is zero.

Syntax

math.atan2(y: number, x: number) -> number

Arguments

ynumberRequired

The vertical coordinate of the point, the rise. It comes first.

xnumberRequired

The horizontal coordinate of the point, the run. It may be zero or negative.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Two absent arguments, or one, give none.

Examples

version 1
study("Phase of a 20 bar cycle", precision = 0, range = [-180, 180])

period = 20
turn   = 2 * math.pi * bar.index / period

// Read the last 20 closes as one wave, cos(turn - phase). The correlation of
// such a wave with the cosine is cos(phase), and with the sine is sin(phase),
// so atan2 of the pair gives the phase back, in the right quarter of the circle.
s = correlation(close, math.sin(turn), period)
c = correlation(close, math.cos(turn), period)

plot(math.toDegrees(math.atan2(s, c)), "Phase, degrees", aqua)

On a close that swings in a clean 20 bar cycle, the line holds steady at that cycle's phase: a wave that peaks 60 degrees after the reference reads 60 on every bar. A line that drifts means the cycle is a little longer or shorter than 20 bars, and one that jumps about means there is no clear 20 bar cycle to read.

CallDegrees
math.atan2(1, 1)45
math.atan2(1, -1)135
math.atan(1 / -1)-45, the wrong quarter for the point (-1, 1)

See also

math.atan(), math.hypot()
html.fn_math.cos:
math.cos()

FunctionIn the guide

The cosine of an angle x in radians, between -1 and 1. Use it to build weights shaped like an arch, or a cycle a quarter turn from a sine.

Syntax

math.cos(x: number) -> number

Arguments

xnumberRequired

The angle, in radians.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

math.cos(0) is 1. The loop above reads close[i], which is absent until there are len bars behind it, so the average has its first value on bar len - 1.

Examples

version 1
study("Hann weighted average", overlay = true)

len = input(20, "Length", min = 3, max = 200)

// Weights shaped like one arch of a cosine: small at both ends of the window
// and largest in the middle.
total  = 0.0
weight = 0.0
for i = 0 to len - 1
    w = 0.5 - 0.5 * math.cos(2 * math.pi * (i + 1) / (len + 1))
    total  += w * close[i]
    weight += w

plot(total / weight, "Hann average", orange)

See also

math.sin(), math.acos(), wma()
html.const_math.e:
math.e

ConstantIn the guide

The number e, about 2.718281828, the base of the natural logarithm. It is a value, not a call: math.e() is error OS2010.

Type

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

pow(math.e, x) is the same as exp(x), and exp() is the shorter way to write it.

Examples

version 1
study("Continuous growth path", overlay = true)

ratePct = input(12, "Growth per year, %", min = 0, max = 100)

var start = close
years = bar.index / 250

// Continuous compounding on a daily chart of about 250 sessions a year.
plot(start * pow(math.e, ratePct / 100 * years), "Growth path", orange)

See also

exp(), log(), math.pi
html.fn_math.hypot:
math.hypot()

FunctionIn the guide

sqrt(x * x + y * y), the length of the line from the origin to (x, y), computed without overflowing on large values. Use it to combine two readings measured on the same scale into one distance.

Syntax

math.hypot(x: number, y: number) -> number

Arguments

xnumberRequired

The first coordinate, or the first of two readings measured on the same scale.

ynumberRequired

The second coordinate, or the second reading. Either argument absent gives none.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

math.hypot(3, 4) is 5. A z-score (a distance from the average counted in standard deviations) puts a price move and a volume on one scale, which is what makes the distance meaningful; adding a raw move in rupees to a raw volume in shares would not be. Either argument absent gives none, so on an instrument without volume the line is not drawn.

Examples

version 1
study("Unusual bar, in move and volume", precision = 2)

len = input(50, "Window, in bars", min = 5, max = 500)

// Two z-scores: how many standard deviations this bar's move and this bar's
// volume sit from their own averages over the window.
move  = change(close)
zMove = (move - sma(move, len)) / stdev(move, len)
zVol  = (volume - sma(volume, len)) / stdev(volume, len)

// The straight line distance from an ordinary bar, where both are zero.
// A bar can reach 3 through either reading alone or through both together.
plot(math.hypot(zMove, zVol), "Distance from an ordinary bar", aqua)
level(3, "Unusual", red)

See also

math.atan2(), sqrt(), stdev()

math.sin()

Arguments

xnumberRequired

The angle, in radians.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

math.sin(math.pi / 2) is 1. The hour and minute are read in the chart's timezone, so on an NSE chart the clock is IST.

version 1
study("Mid-session weight", precision = 2, range = [0, 1])

// Minutes since 09:15, as a share of the 375 minute NSE session:
// 0 at the open and 1 at 15:30.
minutesIn = date.hour(time) * 60 + date.minute(time) - (9 * 60 + 15)

html.fn_math.tan:
math.tan()

FunctionIn the guide

The tangent of an angle x in radians: the rise per unit across of a line at that angle. Use it to turn an angle into a slope.

Syntax

math.tan(x: number) -> number

Arguments

xnumberRequired

The angle, in radians.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

An angle drawn on a chart depends on how the chart is stretched, so a slope in degrees only means something once you fix the scale, as the ATR does here. math.tan(math.pi / 4) gives 0.9999999999999999 rather than exactly 1, because math.pi is a binary number a hair away from the true pi. Examples

version 1
study("Angle to points per bar", precision = 2)

angle = input(45, "Angle, in degrees", min = -89, max = 89)

// On a chart scaled so that one ATR up matches one bar across, a line at
// this angle rises this many points per bar.
plot(math.tan(math.toRadians(angle)) * atr(14), "Points per bar", aqua)

xnumberRequired

html.fn_max:
max()

FunctionIn the guide

The larger of a and b. A second form, max(arr), gives the largest element of an array. Use the two value form for the top of a candle body, a floor under a computed value, or a stop that only moves one way.

Syntax

max(a: number, b: number) -> number
max(arr: array<number>) -> number

Arguments

anumberRequired

The first of the two values to compare.

bnumberRequired

The second value to compare. Either value absent gives none.

arrarray<number>Required

An array of numbers, in the form max(arr), whose largest element is returned. An empty array or an absent element gives none.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Either argument absent gives none, which is why the example seeds stop separately: max(none, candidate) would stay none for ever. The array form follows the same rules as min(): an empty array or an absent element gives none. For the largest value of a series over several bars, use highest().

Examples

version 1
study("Stop that only rises", overlay = true)

candidate = close - 2 * atr(14)

var stop = none
if isNone(stop)
    stop = candidate
else
    stop = max(stop, candidate)

plot(stop, "Rising stop", red, style = "step")

median()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The middle value of src over the last len bars. With an even len it is the mean of the two middle values. Use it as a centre line that one extreme bar cannot drag far.

Syntax

median(src: series number, len: number) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series whose middle value is taken.

lennumberRequired

How many bars the window covers, this bar included. A whole number of 1 or more; with an even count the result is the mean of the two middle values.

Returns

series number

First value: bar len - 1.

Remarks

A single outlier, such as a result day spike, moves the mean by its full size divided by len but barely moves the median. median(src, len) is exactly percentile(src, len, 50).

Examples

version 1
study("Median and mean close", overlay = true)

plot(median(close, 21), "Median 21", orange)

html.fn_mfi:
mfi()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The money flow index is rsi() computed on money flow, the typical price times volume, instead of on price. It reads from 0 to 100, with 80 and 20 as the usual overbought and oversold levels.

Syntax

mfi(len?: number = 14) -> series number

Arguments

lennumberDefault 14

The window, in bars, over which the rising and the falling money flow are summed.

Returns

series number

First value: bar len.

Remarks

Each bar's flow is hlc3 times volume. The flow counts on the rising side when the typical price rose from the previous bar and on the falling side when it fell; an unchanged typical price counts on neither. The result is 100 - 100 / (1 + rising / falling) over window sums, not smoothed averages, and it is 100 when the falling sum is zero. The first value is on bar len.

Examples

version 1
study("Money flow index", precision = 2, range = [0, 100])

m = mfi(14)

plot(m, "MFI", purple, width = 2)
level(80, "Overbought", fade(red, 40))
level(20, "Oversold", fade(lime, 40))

See also

rsi(), cmf()
html.fn_min:
min()

FunctionIn the guide

The smaller of a and b. A second form, min(arr), gives the smallest element of an array. The compiler picks the form from the arguments you pass.

Syntax

min(a: number, b: number) -> number
min(arr: array<number>) -> number

Arguments

anumberRequired

The first of the two values to compare.

bnumberRequired

The second value to compare. Either value absent gives none.

arrarray<number>Required

An array of numbers, in the form min(arr), whose smallest element is returned. An empty array or an absent element gives none.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Either argument absent gives none. The two value form takes exactly two arguments; for three, nest the calls: min(min(a, b), c), or put the values in an array. min([3, 9, 4]) is 3. An empty array has no smallest element, so it gives none, and so does an array holding an absent element. For the smallest value of a series over several bars, use lowest().

Examples

version 1
study("Wicks", precision = 2)

upperWick = high - max(open, close)
lowerWick = min(open, close) - low

plot(upperWick, "Upper wick", red, style = "column")
plot(lowerWick, "Lower wick", lime, style = "column")

See also

max(), clamp(), lowest()
html.fn_mix:
mix()

FunctionIn the guide

A blend of two colours: weight 0 gives a, 1 gives b, and 0.5 gives the colour halfway between. Compute the weight from a value and you have a colour scale, such as candles that grow redder as volume rises.

Syntax

mix(a: color, b: color, weight: number) -> color

Arguments

acolorRequired

The colour at weight 0.

bcolorRequired

The colour at weight 1.

weightnumberRequired

How far to blend from a to b: 0 gives a, 1 gives b and 0.5 the colour halfway. A weight outside 0 to 1 is not refused and carries the blend past the far colour, so clamp it first.

Returns

color

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

All four channels are blended, alpha included. Red, green and blue are then rounded to whole numbers, halves away from zero, so mix(red, blue, 0.3) is #b3004dff. A weight outside 0 to 1 is not refused: the blend carries on past the far colour and each channel is then clamped to its range, which is rarely the colour you meant. Clamp the weight first, as above. An absent weight gives an absent colour.

Examples

version 1
study("Volume heat", overlay = true)

hottest = input(3.0, "Volume multiple that counts as hot", min = 1.5, max = 10)

rv = relativeVolume(20)

// Volume at its average gives 0, volume at the hot multiple gives 1.
// The clamp keeps one enormous bar from pushing the weight past red.
weight = clamp((rv - 1) / (hottest - 1), 0, 1)

// Absent during warmup, which leaves the candles their own colour.
barColor(mix(silver, red, weight))

See also

gradient(), clamp(), barColor()
html.fn_mod:
mod()

FunctionIn the guide

The remainder of a divided by b, taking the sign of b: a - b * floor(a / b). Use it to wrap a value into a cycle, such as the minutes of a session into half hours or an angle into 0 to 360.

Syntax

mod(a: number, b: number) -> number

Arguments

anumberRequired

The number to divide.

bnumberRequired

The number to divide by. The remainder takes its sign, and a b of 0 gives none.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Use mod to wrap a value that can go below zero: mod(angle, 360) always lands from 0 up to 360, so mod(-90, 360) is 270, where -90 % 360 stays at -90. mod(a, 0) gives none, as does a % 0. Fractions work: mod(7.5, 2) is 1.5.

Examples

version 1
study("Half hours from the open", overlay = true)

// Minutes since 09:15, read in the chart's timezone.
sinceOpen = date.hour(time) * 60 + date.minute(time) - (9 * 60 + 15)

// True on the bars that open at 09:15, 09:45, 10:15 and every half hour
// after, on a 1, 5 or 15 minute chart.
halfHour = mod(sinceOpen, 30) == 0
background(halfHour ? fade(silver, 90) : none)

mod and the % operator agree whenever b is positive and a is at or above zero. They differ when a sign is negative, and both exist on purpose:

ExpressionValueSign follows
mod(7, 3)1
7 % 31
mod(-7, 3)2The divisor, 3
-7 % 3-1The left operand, -7
mod(7, -3)-2The divisor, -3
7 % -31The left operand, 7

See also

floor(), Operators

The series whose change is measured.

lennumberDefault 10

Returns

series number

Remarks

The first value is on bar len, the first bar that has a value len bars behind it. It is not smoothed; tsi() is a smoothed relative of it and roc() expresses the same change as a percentage.

len = input(10, "Length", min = 1, max = 200)
m = mom(close, len)

html.var_oi:
oi

VariableIn the guide

Open interest: the number of futures or options contracts outstanding at the end of the bar. It is what lets you read positioning on NFO and MCX contracts, which price and volume alone cannot show.

Type

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

The classic reading: price rising with open interest rising suggests new positions being built, and price rising with open interest falling suggests existing short positions being closed.
