html.fn_stdev:
stdev()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The standard deviation of the last len values: how widely they are spread around their mean, in the source's own units. By default it divides by len (the population form, which is what the band indicators use); pass sample = true to divide by len - 1. A second form takes an array and returns the standard deviation of its elements.

Syntax

stdev(src: series number, len: number, sample?: bool = false) -> series number
stdev(arr: array<number>) -> number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series whose spread is measured.

lennumberRequired

The number of bars in the window.

sampleboolDefault false

Whether to divide by len - 1, the sample form, instead of len, the population form. The band indicators use the population form.

arrarray<number>Required

The array whose elements are measured, in the second form of the call. That form always uses the population divisor.

Returns

series number | number

First value: bar len - 1.

Remarks

The series form computes the mean first and then the squared distances from it, in two passes, which stays accurate on prices where the values are large and the spread is small. The first value is on bar len - 1. The array form always uses the population divisor and returns none for an empty array or one holding an absent element.

Examples

version 1
study("Z-score", precision = 2)

len = input(20, "Length", min = 2, max = 500)

mean = sma(close, len)
dev  = stdev(close, len)
z    = dev > 0 ? (close - mean) / dev : none

plot(z, "Z-score", aqua, width = 2)
level(2, "+2", fade(red, 40))
level(0, "Mean", fade(gray, 60))
level(-2, "-2", fade(lime, 40))

The z-score says how many standard deviations the close sits from its average. The array form works on any list you build:

version 1
study("Spread of the last five closes", precision = 2)

closes = [close, close[1], close[2], close[3], close[4]]

plot(stdev(closes), "Deviation of five closes", silver)

See also

variance(), bollinger(), hv(), Collections
html.fn_stoch:
stoch()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The stochastic oscillator places the close inside the window's range: 100 at the highest high, 0 at the lowest low. It returns [k, d], where %K is the position smoothed over smoothK bars and %D is %K smoothed over smoothD bars. With smoothK of 1 you get the fast stochastic; 3 gives the common slow stochastic.

Syntax

stoch(len?: number = 14, smoothK?: number = 1, smoothD?: number = 3) -> array<number>

Arguments

lennumberDefault 14

The window, in bars, whose highest high and lowest low set the range the close is placed in.

smoothKnumberDefault 1

The number of bars the raw position is averaged over to give %K. 1 gives the fast stochastic and 3 the common slow one.

smoothDnumberDefault 3

The number of bars %K is averaged over to give %D.

Returns

array<number>

First value: element 0 at bar len + smoothK - 2, element 1 at bar len + smoothK + smoothD - 3.

Remarks

The raw position is 100 * (close - lowest low) / (highest high - lowest low) over len bars, using the bars' own highs and lows rather than the highest and lowest close. %K is sma() of that over smoothK and %D is sma() of %K over smoothD. With stoch(14, 3, 3), %K starts on bar 15 and %D on bar 17. The position is absent on a bar where the window's high equals its low.

Examples

version 1
study("Slow stochastic", precision = 2, range = [0, 100])

s = stoch(14, 3, 3)
k = s[0]
d = s[1]

plot(k, "%K", aqua, width = 2)
plot(d, "%D", orange)
level(80, "Overbought", fade(red, 40))
level(20, "Oversold", fade(lime, 40))

if crossUp(k, d) and k < 20
    signal("K UP", color = lime, at = "below", shape = "triangleUp")

See also

stochRsi(), williamsR(), donchian()
html.fn_stochRsi:
stochRsi()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The stochastic RSI applies the stochastic position test to rsi() instead of to price: where does today's RSI sit within its own recent range? It moves faster than RSI and reaches its extremes far more often, so it suits short-term timing. It returns [k, d].

Syntax

stochRsi(
    src: series number,
    rsiLen?: number = 14,
    stochLen?: number = 14,
    smoothK?: number = 3,
    smoothD?: number = 3
) -> array<number>

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series the RSI is computed on, usually close.

rsiLennumberDefault 14

The length of the RSI.

stochLennumberDefault 14

The window, in bars, of RSI values whose high and low set the range the RSI is placed in.

smoothKnumberDefault 3

The number of bars the raw position is averaged over to give %K.

smoothDnumberDefault 3

The number of bars %K is averaged over to give %D.

Returns

array<number>

First value: element 0 at bar rsiLen + stochLen + smoothK - 2.

Remarks

The window's high and low are taken from the RSI values themselves, over stochLen bars. %K starts on bar rsiLen + stochLen + smoothK - 2 and %D follows smoothD - 1 bars later: bars 29 and 31 with the defaults. When RSI makes a new high for the window on bar after bar, the raw reading sits at 100 (and at 0 for a run of new lows), so %K can stay pinned at an extreme through a steady trend. The raw reading is absent when RSI has not moved across the window, since its high then equals its low.

Examples

version 1
study("Stochastic RSI", precision = 2, range = [0, 100])

s = stochRsi(close, 14, 14, 3, 3)

plot(s[0], "%K", aqua, width = 2)
plot(s[1], "%D", orange)
level(80, "High", fade(red, 40))
level(20, "Low", fade(lime, 40))

See also

rsi(), stoch()
html.fn_str.contains:
str.contains()

FunctionIn the guide

True when part appears anywhere inside s, and false when it does not. The test is exact and case sensitive: "NIFTY" does not contain "nifty".

Syntax

str.contains(s: string, part: string) -> bool

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to search in.

partstringRequired

The text to look for. The test is exact and case sensitive, and an empty part is contained in every string.

Returns

bool

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Containment can match more than you meant: "BANKNIFTY" contains "NIFTY". When the part must be at a known end, use str.startsWith() or str.endsWith(). An empty part is contained in every string. To ignore case, convert both sides with str.upper() first.

Examples

// A symbol with BANK in its name, such as BANKNIFTY or HDFCBANK, gets a wider stop.
isBank   = str.contains(chart.symbol, "BANK")
atrValue = atr(14)
plot(isBank ? atrValue * 1.5 : atrValue, "Stop distance")

See also

str.startsWith(), str.endsWith(), str.indexOf()
html.fn_str.endsWith:
str.endsWith()

FunctionIn the guide

True when s ends with part. OpenAlgo writes a futures contract as the underlying, the expiry and FUT (BANKNIFTY24APR24FUT), and an option as the underlying, the expiry, the strike and CE or PE (NIFTY28MAR2420800CE), so a suffix test is a quick way to tell what is on the chart.

Syntax

str.endsWith(s: string, part: string) -> bool

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to test.

partstringRequired

The text the string must end with. The test is case sensitive, and an empty part is a suffix of every string.

Returns

bool

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

A suffix alone can mislead: RELIANCE and BAJFINANCE end in CE as well. That is why the example checks for a digit before the suffix. Case sensitive. An empty part is a suffix of every string. chart.instrumentType reports the kind of instrument directly on a host that supplies it.

Examples

sym = chart.symbol
n   = str.length(sym)

// An option symbol ends in its strike and then CE or PE, as in NIFTY28MAR2420800CE.
// Asking for a digit before those two letters keeps out a stock such as RELIANCE.
strikeBefore = n >= 3 ? not isNone(toNumber(str.substring(sym, n - 3, n - 2))) : false

kind = strikeBefore and str.endsWith(sym, "CE") ? "Call option" :
       strikeBefore and str.endsWith(sym, "PE") ? "Put option" :
       str.endsWith(sym, "FUT") ? "Future" : "Stock or index"

panel = table("Contract", 1, 1)
if bar.isLast
    cell(panel, 0, 0, kind)

See also

str.startsWith(), str.substring(), chart.instrumentType
html.fn_str.indexOf:
str.indexOf()

FunctionIn the guide

The position of the first occurrence of part in s, counting from 0, or -1 when it does not occur. Pair it with str.substring() to cut a string at a separator.

Syntax

str.indexOf(s: string, part: string) -> number

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to search in.

partstringRequired

The text to find. The result is its first position counting from 0, or -1 when it does not occur.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Not found is -1, a definite answer rather than none, so compare the result with -1 or >= 0. The position counts code points. An empty part is found at 0. To split at every separator in one call, use str.split().

Examples

spec  = input("NSE:SBIN", "Instrument, as EXCHANGE:SYMBOL")
colon = str.indexOf(spec, ":")

// Everything after the colon, or the whole text when there is no colon.
symbolPart = colon >= 0 ? str.substring(spec, colon + 1) : spec

panel = table("Instrument", 1, 1)
if bar.isLast
    cell(panel, 0, 0, symbolPart)

See also

str.contains(), str.substring(), str.split(), indexOf()
html.fn_str.join:
str.join()

FunctionIn the guide

Joins the strings in parts into one string, with separator between each pair. It is the reverse of str.split(), and the tidy way to build a line from several fields.

Syntax

str.join(parts: array<string>, separator: string) -> string

Arguments

partsarray<string>Required

The strings to join, in order. An absent element is written as the word none.

separatorstringRequired

The text written between each pair of parts, such as ", ".

Returns

string

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

An empty array joins to the empty string. An absent element is written as the word none, so a field that is still warming up shows as that word rather than making the whole line disappear. To show a running list without growing one huge string, keep the pieces in a var array, trim it, and join only what you show:

// The last five closes, oldest first.
var lines: array<string> = []
push(lines, text(close, 2))
if size(lines) > 5
    shift(lines)

panel = table("Recent closes", 1, 1)
if bar.isLast
    cell(panel, 0, 0, str.join(lines, ", "))

Examples

fields = [chart.symbol, text(open, 2), text(high, 2), text(low, 2), text(close, 2)]

panel = table("Last bar", 1, 1)
if bar.isLast
    cell(panel, 0, 0, str.join(fields, " | "))

See also

str.split(), push(), shift()
html.fn_str.length:
str.length()

FunctionIn the guide

The number of characters in s. Use it to check that a text input is not empty, or to keep a label short enough for the space it has, as the Readings panel above does with a long option symbol.

Syntax

str.length(s: string) -> number

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to measure.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

The rupee sign ₹ counts as one character, like any letter. The empty string "" has a length of 0.

Examples

note  = str.trim(input("", "Note to show"))
panel = table("Note", 1, 1, position = "bottomLeft")

// Write the cell only when the reader typed something.
if bar.isLast and str.length(note) > 0

html.fn_str.lower:
str.lower()

FunctionIn the guide

s with every letter in small letters, on the same fixed terms as str.upper(). Lower-case the text a reader typed before you compare it, so Buy, BUY and buy all match.

Syntax

str.lower(s: string) -> string

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to convert to small letters.

Returns

string

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

For a choice from a fixed list, a menu input with options is better than free text, because the reader cannot mistype it. See input().

Examples

side  = input("Buy", "Side")
isBuy = str.lower(str.trim(side)) == "buy"
plot(isBuy ? low : high, "Reference price")

html.fn_str.padLeft:
str.padLeft()

FunctionIn the guide

s with fill added on the left until it is width characters long. Use it to give a number a fixed count of digits, such as the minutes of a clock time.

Syntax

str.padLeft(s: string, width: number, fill?: string = " ") -> string

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to pad.

widthnumberRequired

The length in characters to pad to. A string already that long or longer comes back unchanged.

fillstringDefault " "

The text added on the left to reach the width. When it is longer than one character it repeats and is cut to fit.

Returns

string

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

A string already width characters or longer comes back unchanged; nothing is cut off. fill defaults to a space and may be longer than one character, in which case it repeats and is cut to fit: str.padLeft("7", 5, "ab") is "abab7". An empty fill adds nothing. A negative or fractional width stops the study at that bar with OS4003.

Examples

// Time left in the 09:15 to 15:30 session, written as h:mm.
minutesIn = (date.hour(time) - 9) * 60 + date.minute(time) - 15
left      = max(375 - minutesIn, 0)
clock     = text(floor(left / 60)) + ":" + str.padLeft(text(left % 60), 2, "0")

panel = table("Session clock", 1, 1)
if bar.isLast
    cell(panel, 0, 0, "Left in the session " + clock)

See also

str.padRight(), text(), cell()
html.fn_str.padRight:
str.padRight()

FunctionIn the guide

s with fill added on the right until it is width characters long. Use it to give a text meter a fixed length, however much of it is filled.

Syntax

str.padRight(s: string, width: number, fill?: string = " ") -> string

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to pad.

widthnumberRequired

The length in characters to pad to. A string already that long or longer comes back unchanged.

fillstringDefault " "

The text added on the right to reach the width. When it is longer than one character it repeats and is cut to fit.

Returns

string

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Follows the same rules as str.padLeft(): a longer string is not cut, and fill repeats to fit, so str.padRight("ab", 5, "xy") is "abxyx".

Examples

r = rsi(close, 14)
filled = isNone(r) ? 0 : round(r / 10)

// Ten characters every time: one # per 10 points of RSI, then dots to fill the rest.
meter = str.padRight(str.repeat("#", filled), 10, ".")

panel = table("RSI meter", 1, 1)
if bar.isLast
    cell(panel, 0, 0, meter)

See also

str.padLeft(), str.repeat()
html.fn_str.repeat:
str.repeat()

FunctionIn the guide

n copies of s joined together. Its main use is a bar drawn out of characters inside a table cell, which shows a size at a glance without a pane of its own.

Syntax

str.repeat(s: string, n: number) -> string

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to repeat.

nnumberRequired

The number of copies, a whole number of 0 or more. A negative or fractional count stops the study with OS4003.

Returns

string

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

n must be a whole number of 0 or more; str.repeat("ab", 0) is "". A negative or fractional n stops the study at that bar with OS4003, so round a computed count first, as above. A very large n can pass the 100,000 character ceiling (OS5008).

Examples

r = rsi(close, 14)
filled = isNone(r) ? 0 : round(r / 5)

panel = table("RSI bar", 1, 1)
if bar.isLast
    cell(panel, 0, 0, "RSI " + str.repeat("|", filled) + str.repeat(".", 20 - filled))

See also

str.padRight(), round(), cell()
html.fn_str.replace:
str.replace()

FunctionIn the guide

s with the first occurrence of find replaced by with. Later occurrences are left alone. It is handy for filling one placeholder in a message template.

Syntax

str.replace(s: string, find: string, with: string) -> string

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to change.

findstringRequired

The text to look for, matched exactly. Only its first occurrence is replaced.

withstringRequired

The text put in place of find.

Returns

string

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

When find does not occur, s comes back unchanged. An empty find matches at position 0, so with is added to the front. To replace every occurrence, use str.replaceAll().

Examples

template = "{symbol}: fast average crossed above slow"
if crossUp(ema(close, 9), ema(close, 21))
    alert(str.replace(template, "{symbol}", chart.symbol), id = "cross-up")

See also

str.replaceAll(), str.format(), alert()
html.fn_str.replaceAll:
str.replaceAll()

FunctionIn the guide

s with every occurrence of find replaced by with, working from left to right. Use it to clean text before you read it, such as removing the commas from a number written the Indian way.

Syntax

str.replaceAll(s: string, find: string, with: string) -> string

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to change.

findstringRequired

The text to look for, matched exactly. Every occurrence is replaced, from left to right.

withstringRequired

The text put in place of each occurrence. It is not searched again.

Returns

string

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

The text you insert is not searched again, so str.replaceAll("aaa", "a", "aa") is "aaaaaa" and cannot run for ever. When find does not occur, s comes back unchanged.

Examples

typed = input("1,00,000", "Capital, in rupees")

// toNumber cannot read the commas, so remove every one of them first.
capital = toNumber(str.replaceAll(typed, ",", ""))

panel = table("Capital", 1, 1)
if bar.isLast
    cell(panel, 0, 0, isNone(capital) ? "Not a number" : text(capital, 0))

See also

str.replace(), toNumber(), str.trim()
html.fn_str.split:
str.split()

FunctionIn the guide

Splits s at every occurrence of separator and returns the pieces as an array of strings. It is the way to accept a list in a single text input, such as a set of price levels.

Syntax

str.split(s: string, separator: string) -> array<string>

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to split.

separatorstringRequired

The text to split at. It is not kept in the pieces, and an empty separator splits the string into single characters.

Returns

array<string>

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

The separator itself is not kept. When it does not occur, the result is one element holding the whole string. Two separators side by side give an empty piece between them, so "a,,b" splits into three parts. An empty separator splits the string into single characters. toNumber() ignores spaces around each number, so "22000, 22250" reads as well as "22000,22250", and an empty or unreadable piece becomes none, which the loop above skips.

Examples

version 1
study("Nearest level", overlay = true)

levelText = input("22000,22250,22500,22750", "Levels, comma separated")

parts = str.split(levelText, ",")
nearest = none
for part in parts
    value = toNumber(part)
    if not isNone(value) and (isNone(nearest) or abs(close - value) < abs(close - nearest))
        nearest = value

plot(nearest, "Nearest level", orange, style = "step")

See also

str.join(), toNumber(), size(), element()

partstringRequired

The text the string must begin with. The test is case sensitive, and an empty part is a prefix of every string.

Returns

bool

Remarks

Case sensitive. An empty part is a prefix of every string.

html.fn_str.substring:
str.substring()

FunctionIn the guide

The part of s from position from up to, but not including, position to. Leave out to to take everything from from to the end. Use it to read fixed fields out of a string, such as the hours and minutes of a session window.

Syntax

str.substring(s: string, from: number, to?: number = none) -> string

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to cut from.

fromnumberRequired

The position to start at, counting from 0. A negative or fractional position stops the study with OS4003.

tonumberDefault none

The position to stop before, which is not included. Left out, everything to the end is taken, and a to past the end is cut back to the end.

Returns

string

A to past the end is cut back to the end, so str.substring("SBIN", 0, 20) is "SBIN". A from at or after to gives the empty string. html.fn_str.trim:
str.trim()

s with the whitespace at both ends removed: spaces, tabs, line breaks and the other Unicode whitespace characters, such as the no-break space. Whitespace inside the string stays. Trim anything a person typed before you compare it or show it.

sstringRequired

The string to trim.

html.fn_str.upper:
str.upper()

FunctionIn the guide

s with every letter in capitals. Use it to show a name in one consistent style, or to compare two strings without caring about case.

str.upper(s: string) -> string

Arguments

sstringRequired

The string to convert to capitals.

Returns

string

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

The conversion is fixed by the language rather than by the language settings of the machine, so it gives the same result everywhere. Letters outside the English alphabet convert too: str.upper("école") is "ÉCOLE".

watch = input("sbin", "Symbol to highlight")

html.fn_sum:
sum()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The total of src over the last len bars, this bar included. A second form, sum(arr), totals every element of an array. The compiler picks the form from the arguments you pass.

Syntax

sum(src: series number, len: number) -> series number
sum(arr: array<number>) -> number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series to total over the window. One absent bar in the window makes the total absent.

lennumberRequired

How many bars the window covers, this bar included. A whole number of 1 or more.

arrarray<number>Required

An array of numbers, in the form sum(arr), whose elements are all added. An empty array totals 0, and an absent element makes the total none.

Returns

series number | number

First value: bar len - 1.

Remarks

In the window form, one absent bar in the window makes the total absent; use sumSkip() to pass over absent bars. In the array form, an empty array totals 0 and an array holding an absent element totals none. A single series with no length matches neither form:

plot(sum(close), "Total")

Examples

version 1
study("Net move over 20 bars", precision = 2)

move = close - open
plot(sum(move, 20), "Sum of bodies, 20 bars", aqua)

The array form reads every element once:

version 1
study("Average of three levels", overlay = true)

levels = [22000.0, 22500.0, 23000.0]
plot(sum(levels) / size(levels), "Average level", orange)

See also

cum(), sumSkip(), count(), avg()
html.fn_sumSkip:
sumSkip()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The total of the present values of src over the last len bars, passing over absent bars. A window with no present values totals 0.

Syntax

sumSkip(src: series number, len: number) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series to total. Bars where it is absent are passed over, and a window with no present values totals 0.

lennumberRequired

How many bars the window covers, this bar included. A whole number of 1 or more.

Returns

series number

First value: bar len - 1.

Remarks

The first value is on bar len - 1, even when the early bars are all absent. Because an empty window totals 0, a zero can mean "nothing present" as well as "the values added to zero"; check countPresent() when the difference matters.

Examples

version 1
study("Up moves and down moves", precision = 2)

upMove   = close > open ? close - open : none
downMove = close < open ? open - close : none

plot(sumSkip(upMove, 20), "Up moves in 20 bars", lime)
plot(sumSkip(downMove, 20), "Down moves in 20 bars", red)

See also

sum(), avgSkip(), countPresent()
html.fn_supertrend:
supertrend()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

A trailing band set a multiple of the average true range away from the bar's midpoint. In an uptrend the line trails below price and only rises; in a downtrend it trails above and only falls. When the close crosses through the line, it flips to the other side. It returns [line, direction], and direction is -1 while the line is below price (long) and 1 while it is above (short).

Syntax

supertrend(factor?: number = 3, atrLen?: number = 10) -> array<number>

Arguments

factornumberDefault 3

How many average true ranges the band sits from the bar's midpoint, hl2. A larger factor gives a looser line that flips less often.

atrLennumberDefault 10

The length of the average true range the band distance is measured in.

Returns

array<number>

First value: element 0 at bar atrLen, element 1 at bar atrLen.

Remarks

The raw bands are hl2 + factor * atr(atrLen) and hl2 - factor * atr(atrLen). From bar to bar the lower band may only rise, unless the previous close fell below it, and the upper band may only fall, unless the previous close rose above it.

The line starts on the upper band, so on a rising chart the first values can read short (1) until the first close above that band flips it. While it follows the upper band it stays there as long as the close is at or below that band; while it follows the lower band it stays as long as the close is at or above it. An exact touch therefore does not flip it.

The first value arrives one bar after atr() has one, on bar atrLen, because the bands need a previous band and a previous close to trail against.

Examples

version 1
study("Supertrend", overlay = true)

factor = input(3.0, "Factor", min = 0.5, max = 10, step = 0.5)
atrLen = input(10, "ATR length", min = 1, max = 100)

st   = supertrend(factor, atrLen)
band = st[0]
dir  = st[1]

plot(dir == -1 ? band : none, "Up trend", lime, width = 2)
plot(dir == 1 ? band : none, "Down trend", red, width = 2)

if dir == -1 and dir[1] == 1
    signal("LONG", color = lime, at = "below", shape = "triangleUp")
if dir == 1 and dir[1] == -1
    signal("SHORT", color = red, at = "above", shape = "triangleDown")

A Supertrend with the same settings on a BHEL 15 minute chart, from a study that also shades between the line and the candles and labels each flip BUY or SELL in place of a triangle:

The example plots the line twice, once per direction, so each flip leaves a gap instead of a vertical jump across the candles. The flip tests compare with dir[1], which is absent on the line's first bar; == against an absent value is false, so no flip is marked there.

See also

psar(), atr(), barColor(), signal()
html.fn_swma:
swma()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The symmetric weighted moving average is a fixed four-bar smoothing with weights 1, 2, 2 and 1. It has no length to set. Use it to take the jitter out of an oscillator or a noisy series while adding only a bar and a half of lag.

Syntax

swma(src: series number) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series to smooth. The average always covers four bars, so there is no length to set.

Returns

series number

First value: bar 3.

Remarks

The result is (w3 + 2 * w2 + 2 * w1 + w0) / 6, where w0 is this bar's value and w3 the value three bars back. It needs four values, so it starts on bar 3 of its source: on rsi(close, 14), which starts on bar 14, it starts on bar 17.

Examples

version 1
study("Smoothed RSI", precision = 2, range = [0, 100])

r = rsi(close, 14)

plot(r, "RSI", fade(purple, 60))
plot(swma(r), "RSI, smoothed", purple, width = 2)
level(70, "Overbought", fade(red, 40))
level(30, "Oversold", fade(lime, 40))

See also

wma(), sma()
html.fn_table:
table()

FunctionTop level onlyIn the guide

Declares a grid of rows by cols cells pinned to one corner of the study's pane, and returns the table that cell() writes into. The title names the grid; the size and corner are part of the study's fixed shape, which is why the call is top level only and every argument is settled before the first bar.

Syntax

table(
    title: string,
    rows: number,
    cols: number,
    position?: string = "topRight",
    textColor?: color = none,
    bgColor?: color = none,
    borderWidth?: number = 0
) -> table

Arguments

titlestringRequired

Names the grid. The /trading chart does not show the title.

Fixed before the first bar.

rowsnumberRequired

The number of rows. Rows are addressed from 0, so a grid of 4 rows has rows 0 to 3.

A whole number. Fixed before the first bar.

colsnumberRequired

The number of columns, addressed from 0 like the rows.

A whole number. Fixed before the first bar.

positionstringDefault "topRight"

The corner of the pane the grid is pinned to: "topLeft", "topRight", "bottomLeft" or "bottomRight". An input() with the four corners as options lets the reader move it.

One of "topLeft", "topRight", "bottomLeft", "bottomRight". Fixed before the first bar.

textColorcolorDefault none

The text colour of every cell that sets none of its own.

Fixed before the first bar.

bgColorcolorDefault none

The grid's background, behind every cell that sets none of its own. A translucent colour such as fade(black, 25) keeps the candles behind the grid faintly visible.

Fixed before the first bar.

borderWidthnumberDefault 0

The thickness of the grid's border, with 0 for no border.

Fixed before the first bar.

Returns

table

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

rows and cols are whole numbers; a fraction is error OS3004. Make position an input() with the four corners as options, since which corner is free depends on the reader's chart. The table is an ordinary value: you can name it, keep it and pass it to a function of your own, and it is never deleted. Writing no cells leaves every cell blank, but the grid keeps its size, its border and its own bgColor, so a grid with a background still shows as an empty block. For a panel the reader can switch off, leave the grid's bgColor and borderWidth out, set bgColor on the cells instead, and guard the writes with if bar.isLast and showPanel. A table with fifty rows of history works and is unreadable at the size of a chart corner; a list belongs in a report, not on the chart.

Examples

version 1
study("Timeframe bias", overlay = true)

tfA = input("15m", "Timeframe 1", kind = "interval")
tfB = input("1h",  "Timeframe 2", kind = "interval")
tfC = input("1D",  "Timeframe 3", kind = "interval")

grid = table("Bias", 4, 2, position = "topRight", bgColor = fade(black, 20), borderWidth = 1)

// Each row changes when that timeframe's bar closes, and not before.
// A timeframe finer than the chart's stops the study with OS6002, so run
// this on a chart of 15 minutes or less.
biasA = req.timeframe(tfA, ema(close, 20) > ema(close, 50))
biasB = req.timeframe(tfB, ema(close, 20) > ema(close, 50))
biasC = req.timeframe(tfC, ema(close, 20) > ema(close, 50))

fn word(b) => isNone(b) ? "warming up" : (b ? "up" : "down")
fn tint(b) => isNone(b) ? silver : (b ? lime : red)

if bar.isLast
    cell(grid, 0, 0, "Timeframe", textColor = white)
    cell(grid, 0, 1, "Bias", textColor = white, align = "right")
    cell(grid, 1, 0, tfA)
    cell(grid, 1, 1, word(biasA), textColor = tint(biasA), align = "right")
    cell(grid, 2, 0, tfB)
    cell(grid, 2, 1, word(biasB), textColor = tint(biasB), align = "right")
    cell(grid, 3, 0, tfC)
    cell(grid, 3, 1, word(biasC), textColor = tint(biasC), align = "right")

A table() inside an if, a loop or a function is error OS3006:

if bar.isLast
    panel = table("Readings", 2, 2)

Its arguments are fixed before the first bar, so write each one at the call as a literal, a colour such as fade(black, 25), or an input(). An argument that depends on bar data is error OS3003, and so is a size held in a name, such as n = 3 followed by table("Readings", n, 2).

See also

cell(), clear(), bar.isLast, Tables

teal

html.fn_tema:
tema()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The triple exponential moving average applies the same lag correction twice: 3 * e1 - 3 * e2 + e3, where e1 is the ema of the source, e2 the ema of e1 and e3 the ema of e2. It is the fastest of the exponential family and the most prone to overshoot.

Syntax

tema(src: series number, len: number) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series to average, such as close or another indicator's output.

lennumberRequired

The length of each of the three chained exponential averages.

Returns

series number

First value: bar 3 * len - 3.

Remarks

Three chained averages need three warmups, so the first value is on bar 3 * len - 3, bar 57 for a length of 20. trix() measures the rate of change of the same triple smoothing.

Examples

version 1
study("Triple EMA trend", overlay = true)

len = input(20, "Length", min = 1, max = 200)
t = tema(close, len)

plot(t, "TEMA", t > t[1] ? teal : maroon, width = 2)

See also

dema(), ema(), trix()
html.fn_text:
text()

FunctionIn the guide

Turns a value into text, for a label, a table cell or an alert message. With one argument it takes any value; with a second, decimals, it writes a number with exactly that many digits after the point.

Syntax

text(x: any) -> string
text(x: number, decimals: number) -> string

Arguments

xanyRequired

The value to write as text, of any type. In the form with decimals it must be a number.

decimalsnumberRequired

How many digits to write after the point, exactly, rounding halves away from zero. A whole number.

Returns

string

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

The two forms treat none differently. text(none) is the four letters "none", which is useful while debugging. text(x, 2) with an absent x is none, and so is any string it is joined to with +, so guard a message during warmup, as the page's first example does with isNone().

A decimal that looks like a half is not always stored as one. 1.005 is held as a number a hair below it, so text(1.005, 2) is "1.00", not "1.01".

Examples

version 1
study("Close and ATR", overlay = true)

a = atr(14)
if bar.isLast
    msg = chart.symbol + " closed at " + text(close, 2) + ", ATR " + text(a, 2)
    draw.label(time, high, msg, textColor = white)
Valuetext(x) writes
A numberThe shortest digits that read back as the same number: 100, 1234.5678, 0.05, 0.3333333333333333. Exponent form only below 0.000001 or from 10 to the 21st up, such as 1e-7 or 1e21
A bool"true" or "false"
A stringThe string itself
A colourHex with alpha, such as "#ff0000ff" for red
none"none"

text(x, decimals) rounds halves away from zero and always writes plain digits, never an exponent: text(1234.5, 0) is "1235", text(-2.5, 0) is "-3" and text(2.5, 2) is "2.50". decimals must be a whole number.

See also

str.padLeft(), date.format(), cell()
html.var_time:
time

VariableIn the guide

The instant the bar opened, as a number of milliseconds since 1 January 1970 in UTC. Because it is an ordinary number, you can subtract two times to get an elapsed duration, compare a bar's time with a date you built, or store it to find a bar again later.

Type

series number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

The number is the same everywhere; turning it into a date or a clock time depends on a timezone. The date functions read it in the chart's timezone by default, which is Asia/Kolkata on the /trading chart, so date.hour(time) of the first NSE bar is 9 and date.minute(time) is 15.

Store time, not bar.index, when you want to recognise a bar later. A bar index shifts when more history loads; a time does not.

Examples

version 1
study("Minutes since the day's first bar", precision = 0)

newDay = bar.isFirst or not date.isSameDay(time, time[1])
var dayStart = none
if newDay
    dayStart = time

plot((time - dayStart) / 60000, "Minutes since the day's first bar", aqua, style = "step")

See also

date.format(), date.hour(), chart.now(), session.isIn()
html.fn_toBool:
toBool()

FunctionIn the guide

Turns a bool that may be absent into a definite one: none becomes false, and true and false stay as they are. Use it where a condition computed during warmup must read as a plain false rather than unknown.

Syntax

toBool(x: any) -> bool

Arguments

xanyRequired

The condition to make definite: none becomes false, and true and false stay as they are. A number is not accepted.

Returns

bool

First value: bar 0, whatever its arguments.

Remarks

The difference shows wherever none would otherwise travel: not (close > ema50) is none during warmup, while not toBool(close > ema50) is true. Choose deliberately, because a warmup bar that reads as false is a claim about the market that nobody measured.

It is not a way to read a number as a condition; there is no truthiness (no rule that treats 0 as false) in the language. In release 0.5.0 the compiler accepts a number or a string here, and the result is false whatever the value, so toBool(1) is false. Write the comparison you mean, such as n != 0. The call is spelled toBool because bool is a type name and cannot be called: bool(x) is OS1019.

Examples

version 1
study("Trend flag", overlay = true)

ema50 = ema(close, 50)
above = toBool(close > ema50)    // false, not none, while the EMA warms up

panel = table("Trend", 1, 2, position = "topRight")
if bar.isLast
    cell(panel, 0, 0, "Above the 50 EMA")
    cell(panel, 0, 1, text(above))

See also

isNone(), text()
html.fn_toNumber:
toNumber()

FunctionIn the guide

Reads a number out of a string, and gives none when the string is not a number. Its most common use is a setting typed as text, such as a list of price levels in one input.

Syntax

toNumber(s: string) -> number

Arguments

sstringRequired

The text to read a number from, such as a value typed into a text input. Text that is not a number gives none.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

It takes a string: toNumber(close) is OS3011. Always test the result with isNone() before you rely on it, as the example does, because a typing slip in a setting gives none rather than an error.

Examples

version 1
study("Distance to the nearest level", precision = 2)

raw = input("22000, 22500, 23000", "Levels, separated by commas")

var levels: array<number> = []
if bar.isFirst
    for part in str.split(raw, ",")
        value = toNumber(part)
        if not isNone(value)
            push(levels, value)

nearest = none
for lvl in levels
    if isNone(nearest) or abs(close - lvl) < abs(close - nearest)
        nearest = lvl

plot(close - nearest, "Distance to the nearest level")
TexttoNumber gives
"12.5", " 12.5 "12.5. Spaces at either end are ignored
"-3", "+3", ".5", "12."-3, 3, 0.5, 12
"2.5e3"2500
"12.5%", "1,234", "0x10", "1_000"none
"", "NaN", "Infinity"none

See also

text(), str.split(), str.trim()
html.fn_trix:
trix()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

TRIX is the one-bar percentage change of a triple exponential average. The triple smoothing filters out short swings, so TRIX turns only on sustained changes of direction. The values are small, so give the study a few extra decimals.

Syntax

trix(src: series number, len?: number = 18) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series that is triple smoothed, usually close.

lennumberDefault 18

The length of each of the three chained exponential averages.

Returns

series number

First value: bar 3 * len - 2.

Remarks

It is 100 * (e3 - e3[1]) / e3[1], where e3 is ema(ema(ema(src, len), len), len). That is the percentage change of the average, not the change of its logarithm. The first value is on bar 3 * len - 2, bar 52 for a length of 18.

Examples

version 1
study("TRIX", precision = 4)

len = input(18, "Length", min = 1, max = 100)
t = trix(close, len)

plot(t, "TRIX", fuchsia, width = 2)
plot(ema(t, 9), "Signal", orange)
level(0, "Zero", fade(gray, 60))

See also

tema(), roc()
html.fn_trueRange:
trueRange()

FunctionIn the guide

True range is the bar's full range including any gap from the previous close: the largest of high - low, abs(high - previous close) and abs(low - previous close). It is the building block of atr(), and on NSE, where most gaps happen at the 09:15 open, it captures the overnight move that high - low misses.

Syntax

trueRange() -> series number

Returns

series number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

On the chart's first bar there is no previous close, so the result there is high - low. This is the one deliberate exception in the library to absence spreading from a missing value: the bar's own range is a true statement about that bar, and it lets atr() start on bar len - 1.

Examples

version 1
study("True range and gaps", precision = 2)

tr     = trueRange()
gapped = tr > high - low

plot(tr, "True range", gapped ? orange : silver, style = "column")

When the true range is larger than the bar's own range, the previous close lay outside this bar: price gapped. The example colours those bars orange.

See also

atr(), natr(), chop()

trunc()

FunctionIn the guide

x with its fraction removed, rounding toward zero: trunc(1.7) is 1 and trunc(-1.7) is -1. Use it when a value should shrink toward zero on both sides alike.

Syntax

trunc(x: number) -> number

Arguments

xnumberRequired

The number whose fraction is removed, rounding toward zero on both sides.

Returns

number

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

For values at or above zero, trunc and floor() agree; they differ only below zero.

Examples

version 1
study("Whole ATRs from the average", precision = 0)

avg20    = ema(close, 20)
distance = (close - avg20) / atr(14)

// trunc treats both sides alike: 1.7 ATRs above and 1.7 below both count
// as one whole ATR.
plot(trunc(distance), "Whole ATRs", aqua, style = "column")

See also

floor(), ceil()
html.fn_tsi:
tsi()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The true strength index smooths the bar-to-bar change twice, then divides by the size of the change smoothed the same way. The result, between -100 and 100, is a clean reading of the direction of momentum without the noise of mom().

Syntax

tsi(src: series number, longLen?: number = 25, shortLen?: number = 13) -> series number

Arguments

srcseries numberRequired

The series whose bar-to-bar change is smoothed, usually close.

longLennumberDefault 25

The length of the first exponential smoothing, applied to the change and to its size.

shortLennumberDefault 13

The length of the second exponential smoothing, applied to the output of the first.

Returns

series number

First value: bar longLen + shortLen - 1.

Remarks

The reading is 100 * ema(ema(change, longLen), shortLen) / ema(ema(abs(change), longLen), shortLen), with the long length applied first. The first value is on bar longLen + shortLen - 1, bar 37 with the defaults. A signal line is not part of the call; the example makes one with ema().

Examples

version 1
study("True strength index", precision = 2)

t   = tsi(close, 25, 13)
sig = ema(t, 7)

plot(t, "TSI", teal, width = 2)
plot(sig, "Signal", orange)
level(0, "Zero", fade(gray, 60))

See also

mom(), ema(), macd()
html.fn_ultimateOsc:
ultimateOsc()

FunctionKeeps stateIn the guide

The ultimate oscillator blends buying pressure over three windows, 7, 14 and 28 bars by default, so that no single length dominates. It reads from 0 to 100, with 70 and 30 as the usual overbought and oversold levels.

Syntax

ultimateOsc(len1?: number = 7, len2?: number = 14, len3?: number = 28) -> series number

Arguments

len1numberDefault 7

The first window, in bars. Its pressure ratio carries a weight of 4 in 7, so pass the shortest length here.

len2numberDefault 14

The second window, in bars. Its pressure ratio carries a weight of 2 in 7.

len3numberDefault 28

The third window, in bars. Its pressure ratio carries a weight of 1 in 7, so pass the longest length here.

Returns

series number

First value: bar max(len1, len2, len3).

Remarks

Buying pressure is close - min(low, previous close) and the bar's range is max(high, previous close) - min(low, previous close). At each length the window sum of pressure is divided by the window sum of range, and the three ratios are blended as 100 * (4 * short + 2 * middle + long) / 7, the shortest window weighted most. Both terms need the previous close, so the first value is on bar max(len1, len2, len3), bar 28 by default.

Examples

version 1
study("Ultimate oscillator", precision = 2, range = [0, 100])

u = ultimateOsc(7, 14, 28)

plot(u, "UO", orange, width = 2)
level(70, "Overbought", fade(red, 40))
level(30, "Oversold", fade(lime, 40))

See also

stoch(), rsi()
html.fn_unshift:
unshift()

FunctionIn the guide

Adds v to the front of the array, so element 0 is always the newest value.

Syntax

unshift(arr: array<E>, v: E) -> nothing

Arguments

arrarray<E>Required

The array to add to.

vERequired

The value to add at the front, where it becomes element 0.

Returns

nothing

First value: bar 0.

Remarks

Every existing element moves up one index. For a window with the oldest value first, use push() and shift() instead.

Examples

var recent: array<number> = []
unshift(recent, close)
if size(recent) > 5
    pop(recent)

// recent[0] is this bar's close, recent[4] the close four bars ago.
